LOANS IN REGINA, ETC.
speechtext:
1.	How many loans have been approved by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Regina, under the new National Housing Act as of June 1, 1954?
2.	How is the lending value on a house established (a) when the house is built for speculative sale to the general public: (b) when the house is built as a result of a contract entered into by the home purchaser and contractor?
3.	Does Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation exercise any control over prices charged by builders for homes financed under the National Housing Act?
4.	Are chartered banks permitted to require a deposit of from $300 to $400 over and above the down payment before approving loans for home construction under the National Housing Act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: LOANS IN REGINA, ETC.
speechtext:
1.	Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have given undertakings to insure 24 loans.
2.	(a) The lending value on a house including land is established by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation after appraisal of the applicant's plan, specifications and the location of the proposed structure. The rates used in the appraisal are computed for each branch office and are based on a fair cost for the area.
(b) Same as for (a).
3.	The maximum selling price for houses built by builders for sale and financed under the National Housing Act is determined by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and is generally in the same amount as the lending value. The amount of the loan is conditional upon the sale of the house to a home purchaser at a price not in excess of the maximum selling price so determined. If the house is sold by the builder at a price exceeding the determined selling price, the amount of the loan is reduced to not more than 90 per cent of the approved loan.
4.	Under the National Housing Act an approved lender is not restricted from taking additional security. Where the applicant is building his own house, by contract or otherwise, it is the policy of most approved lenders to require that the applicants have cash or its equivalent available in excess of the difference between the estimated cost
and the mortgage loan, to meet the contingency that most houses cost more than home owners expect. The amounts of this requirement vary and are determined between the borrower and the approved lender.

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: Could the Minister of Trade and Commerce give the house any information concerning the decision of the United States federal power commission announced yesterday which appears to make it impossible for Canada to export natural gas to the northwestern states? I have in mind particularly whether the government has given consideration to making any protest to the United States government in view of the fact that the decision seems to be based in part at least on broad government policy, and also whether this need necessarily prevent Peace river gas being supplied to British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext:
The ruling of the federal power commission has been brought down denying the application of Westcoast Transmission Company Limited to supply gas to the Pacific coast states. I suppose the finding of the commission is comparable to a finding of the board of transport commissioners in

Inquiries of the Ministry Canada, namely, it represents a judicial decision. I hardly think a protest by this government would be effective. I have not seen the judgment but I am told that the chairman of the commission made a report in which he dissented in part from the finding and suggested that Canada apply for permission to export gas to the inland empire, that is the area around Spokane. I have not read the report, but I was informed of that fact by one of my officials.
The government of Canada did everything possible to facilitate the application. Any suggestion from the company that government action would help was followed by action on the part of the government. I myself called on the federal power commission in the hope that I could resolve any doubts they may have had about the Canadian position. I had a very satisfactory interview with the full commission.
Answering the second part of the question, there is nothing to prevent gas being transmitted to Trail and Vancouver except the question whether the volume of gas will be sufficient to allow the gas to be delivered at a price that will be interesting to the purchasers.

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: I was very interested in the minister's explanation. In view of the great need for co-operation between Canada and the United States in the development of the resources of northwestern America, particularly the resources of the Columbia river, can the minister say whether the federal power commission gave any consideration to the necessity for this very close co-operation between the two countries when dealing with this application?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: I suppose the doubt expressed by the federal power commission about the wisdom of having a source of supply outside their own country is similar to doubts I have heard expressed in the House of Commons about the wisdom of bringing gas to Toronto from Buffalo. Such doubts are somewhat natural. I was hoping that the geographical and other facts of the situation would overcome that natural feeling. Apparently they did not. However, the matter will be explored and if there is anything the government can do to improve the situation I can assure you that it will be done.

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext:
May I ask the minister if he would feel himself in a position to comment on the likelihood or possibility of some tie-up being made of the Pacific Northwest Company's pipe line with Westcoast Transmission so that even though the pipe line in the Pacific northwestern states was that of the Pacific Northwest Company, Westcoast's 

line might bring gas down from the Peace river through British Columbia to supplement it in the feeding of that market, which would of course have tremendous advantage for us in the interior of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: That would seem to me to be a possibility, but it is a matter for private negotiations. As I read the newspaper statement, the decision is based on the fact that the federal power commission did not like to make a foreign source of supply the sole source of gas for the area. Possibly, if the area has a domestic supply, that can be supplemented later by a supply from Canada. Obviously, that is a matter for private negotiations.

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: But there is no difficulty in the way from this end?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce? I was puzzled by what he said about the decision being a judicial one. Would he add a word of explanation to that? It would seem to me as if, in effect, although superficially it is different, it is a matter of trade policy. Does the minister not agree with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: The federal power commission is a court, having the jurisdiction of a court, just as the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada is a court, having the powers of a court. I understand that the findings of the federal power commission represent a judicial decision just as the findings of the board of transport commissioners do. I believe the two are on exactly the same footing.

maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: Would it not be necessary, going behind that, for the federal power commission to be reaching a conclusion on instructions received from the government as a matter of policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DECISION OF FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION AGAINST EXPORT TO NORTHWESTERN STATES
speechtext: I cannot say as to that; that is a matter within the United States. Certainly I think that we in Canada could not influence the situation.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of press reports from the 47-nation
Inquiries of the Ministry conference now taking place in London in relation to the international wheat agreement that representatives of the importing countries are seeking a new agreement and that Canadian representatives are understood to express approval of the proposal, can the minister inform the house about the present status of those negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT
speechtext: The meeting of the international wheat agreement countries, Mr. Speaker, is purely a routine meeting. I understand, though I have not been officially advised, that at the meeting a proposal was made that discussions take place in the near future about a further agreement; that is an agreement to succeed the present agreement when it expires within two years. The thought has been expressed that the new agreement might replace the last year of the present agreement. I have no official information on the subject. Canada has not given its delegate instructions on the point, and he has not asked for instructions, from which I take it that the proposal is only in the discussion stage at the moment.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT
speechtext: In view of the fact that we have had so much discussion concerning wheat marketing, and that there have been some indications of discussions relating to a change in the agreement prior to the ordinary termination and a possible relationship of that to price, could the Minister of Trade and Commerce take this as notice of a question to see if information could be obtained through ordinary government channels so that the house could be informed on Monday regarding such information as may be available?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT
speechtext: I assume that by Monday we will have information from our delegate. If it is information that bears on the price of wheat or the duration of the agreement, I shall be glad to make a statement.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question? In view of the small percentage of the agreed imports by importing countries having been taken up, and as this vitally affects Canadian exports, is the minister considering going to London to take part in the discussions before the meeting adjourns?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I think it should be made clear that, unless wheat is put at the floor price specified in the agreement, there is no obligation on the member countries to take their full allotment. I have tried to make that clear on a number of occasions. The choice we have today is whether or not we will offer wheat at the

Supply-Veterans Affairs floor in order that countries will be required to take up their allotment. My feeling is definitely against doing so, but until we do offer wheat at the minimum there is no obligation on those countries to take any more wheat than they desire to take for their own reasons. The fact of the matter is that every country within the wheat agreement had a good crop last year and the requirements for wheat from outside sources are down.

DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS Treatment services-
512. Hospital construction, improvements, new equipment and acquisition of land, $5,300,000.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
This item is for hospital construction, so I should like to say a word about the situation in Calgary in connection with the Colonel Belcher hospital, a veterans affairs hospital. This hospital is in process of being considerably enlarged, so that it will take in more than a full block. There is a piece of property, the Hull estate right next to it, that has just been put on the market. I would ask the minister if he would consider whether the Department of Veterans Affairs would buy this property to make a park outside as a place where patients in the veterans hospital could go, and where they might take their wheelchairs, or such other means as they have for getting around. There is a park right across from the veterans hospital, but it requires crossing a heavy traffic artery. There is a subway just below leading into the centre of the city, and the traffic there is extremely heavy.

As a result the veterans from the hospital do not use Central park in Calgary to any extent, because they find it impractical to use it.
The other piece of property to which I am referring is in the other direction and would be right next to the hospital. I should think it would be a most desirable move if the department would secure that piece of property so that it could be used as a park by the veterans in the hospital, and also would be available for future building purposes if required.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for advising me of that situation and I shall be pleased to have the officials of the department look into the matter.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Has the minister considered building a hospital in Saskatchewan for the mentally disabled. I understand there are about 400 of them, and that Saskatchewan is the only province that does not have suitable mental care provided by the D.V.A. I understand the situation in that province, so far as the mentally disabled are concerned, is somewhat pathetic, as they are scattered all over the province, and not in any separate institutions. In view of the fact that every other province has such care I suggest the mentally defective in Saskatchewan should be treated in the same way.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I am afraid the information the hon. member has concerning institutions for mental patients is not quite accurate. Actually we have two psychiatric institutions, one at Ste. Anne de Bellevue in Montreal and the other at Westminster hospital, in London. Some of the other large hospitals have psychiatric wards, but the only mental institutions are the two I have mentioned. However, in the other provinces, we have arrangements with the provincial authorities whereby they make available to the Department of Veterans Affairs facilities in their mental institutions, at the charge which is current in the province for such institutions.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
In asking my question I have before me a letter from the Saskatchewan hospitals branch of the Canadian Legion at North Battleford in which it is claimed that in all other provinces, to the best of their knowledge, there are at least parts of hospitals-indeed if not whole institutions-set aside for this purpose. They make reference to the Shaughnessy hospital in British Columbia, the Colonel Belcher hospital in Alberta, the Deer Lodge in Manitoba, the Sunnybrook in Ontario, as well as the Westminster in that province. Then they also refer

to the hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Quebec. They claim that Saskatchewan alone has no hospital of this kind.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I am afraid that in this instance the branch of the Legion is wrong.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Would the minister give information as to the number of beds occupied in hospitals, on an average.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
We have Camp Hill hospital at Halifax with an operating capacity of 550 beds, of which at the present time 416 are occupied. There is Lancaster hospital in Lancaster, a municipality which has just been recently organized near Saint John. In that hospital there is a capacity of 400 beds of which 362 are occupied at the present time. There is Ste. Foy hospital in Quebec city. This is a new hospital opened only a few weeks ago. It has a bed capacity of 275, of which 132 are now occupied.
Then, in Montreal, there is Queen Mary veterans hospital with a bed capacity of 700 beds of which 489 are occupied. There is also the hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue with a bed capacity of 1,135 of which 1,094 are occupied. There is the hospital at St. Hyacinthe, Quebec, which is, in fact, a hospital treating tuberculosis. It is being handed over this summer to the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the patients at St. Hyacinthe will be cared for at Ste. Anne de Bellevue; so that the bed capacity at Ste. Anne de Bellevue will be slightly increased. The hospital at St. Hyacinthe had a capacity of 200.
Then, in Ottawa, we have the Rideau health and occupational centre with a capacity of 150 beds, of which 117 are occupied. At Toronto there is Sunny brook hospital with a bed capacity of 1,650 of which 1,235 are occupied. There is also the Red Chevron at Toronto with a bed capacity of 165, with 139 occupied. In London, Ontario, there is the Westminster hospital with a capacity of 1,522 of which 1,237 are occupied.
In Winnipeg we have Deer Lodge hospital with a bed capacity of 850 of which 627 are occupied. In Regina there is the veterans home with a bed capacity of 62, and 63 occupied. Just where that one bed comes in, I cannot say; it must be in the hall.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Out in the corridor.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
There is the veterans hospital at Saskatoon with a bed capacity of 125 with an occupancy of 118. At Calgary there is the Colonel Belcher hospital with a bed capacity of 425 of which 338 are occupied. At Edmonton there is the veterans home with a capacity of 70 and 72 occupied. So that here, again, there must be two out in the hallways.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
At Vancouver there is the Shaughnessy hospital with a bed capacity of 1,100 of which 906 are occupied. There is the veterans hospital at Victoria with a capacity of 300 with 247 occupied. There is the George Derby health and occupational centre at Burnaby, British Columbia, with a capacity of 215 beds, of which 169 are occupied.
Then I must explain that in addition to these institutions we have what we call contract hospitals. For instance, here in Ottawa, we have the veterans pavilion at the Civic hospital, where we enter into a contract with that particular civil hospital for the treatment of veterans. We have a similar arrangement at Regina, Edmonton, Newfoundland and Charlottetown.
The total bed capacity in departmental institutions and contract hospitals, if I may use that term, shows an operating capacity of 9,974 with an occupancy at the present time of 7,935, or an average of about 80 per cent.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Is there any intention on the part of the department to establish a nurses' residence at Camp Hill hospital in Halifax? I do not want to go into the details of the thing, but the nurse who has to room out and take a couple of meals in hospital, for which she is charged, I understand, and lose the time that she has to put in to get out, to get through the traffic and to get back to work, is working under a handicap. I am of the opinion that there is a sufficient number of nurses there to have proper residences provided for them and better arrangements with regard to meals, and so on.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: No such plans have been made up to the present time. As a matter of fact, I am informed that the majority of nurses do not want to reside in the hospital, but prefer to live outside. However, I shall be glad to look into the situation, and certainly we have no intention of creating any hardship for the personnel of our hospitals.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I would be glad if the minister would do that, because the system is antiquated; it is out of date.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
I have a matter that I should like to bring to the minister's attention under this item. I refer to the provision of a veterans pavilion at the Lethbridge hospital. I believe the Lethbridge branch of the Legion and some other branches of the Legion in southern Alberta, as well as other bodies, have made representations to the minister in regard to the desirability of providing a veterans pavilion at the Lethbridge hospital which would serve a good many of the people in the far southern part of Alberta. At the present time they all have to go up to the

Supply-Veterans Affairs Colonel Belcher, where they are separated a long distance from their families and so on. The population of that part of Alberta of course, owing to the irrigation schemes which have gone in there, has been increasing rapidly and they believe they have a sufficient number of veterans to justify the provision of a veterans pavilion at the Lethbridge hospital. Can the minister tell us-he was going to consider this-what has been the result of the investigation, if any, into the matter?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Some time ago representations were made to the effect that a veterans pavilion should be set up at the Lethbridge hospital. I think those are the representations to which my hon. friend refers.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: At that time we did make a thorough investigation. The result of that investigation was that the patient load in such a veterans pavilion would not be sufficient to warrant the expense of setting up one. My hon. friend says that circumstances may have changed because of various developments, and I shall be very glad to look into the question again, to find out the best way of giving the best treatment to the veterans of that region. The department certainly will look into this matter very seriously.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I have another question along the line of the last. Do the accounting practices of the department leave the minister in a position to estimate the cost of maintenance per bed? Has that cost been compared with the corresponding cost in the public civilian hospitals as a method of testing the departmental costs?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Yes, there is a thorough system of cost accounting with respect to our hospital operations, and the daily rate per person is calculated for each institution. The comparison of such costs is made with civilian institutions; but, of course, in our accounting we take into consideration certain services which are not usually considered in the cost accounting of civilian institutions, because they charge their patients for such items as laboratory tests, X-rays and medical services. Under our system we include all these items in the daily rate for each patient in a hospital.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Can the minister give us the average cost per patient per day say over the last year?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
The daily rate broken down for 1953 was $12.55 per patient. To give a basis of comparison with civilian institutions, I might add that the rate in general hospitals

in Ontario, where we do have patients receiving treatment under contracts with these hospitals is $13.31 per patient day, exclusive of the cost of medical services.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Does that figure of $12.55 include medical services?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: It does.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: In the figures that the minister gave us a while ago, it was indicated that there are somewhere around 2,000 unoccupied beds in military hospitals across Canada. Has any consideration been given to the possibility of making some of those unoccupied beds available to the civilian population? In Toronto, for instance, there is a desperate shortage of civilian beds. There are thousands of civilian patients on waiting lists to get into hospital. These military hospitals are maintained at the public expense. Why should there be several hundred unoccupied beds in Sunnybrook hospital, while thousands of civilian patients in Toronto are seeking hospital accommodation. Sunnybrook hospital has, I suppose, some of the best equipment, and probably the best staff in Canada, for certain types of rehabilitation work. I do not know whether that is used to the fullest extent, but it would seem to me that it should be possible to make some arrangements with municipalities whereby people who want hospital accommodation should be able to get it when hospital accommodation is being unused a few blocks away.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
That matter has been looked into very thoroughly. At the beginning I should say that it is not considered that a hospital should at all times be a hundred per cent occupied. There has to be some flexibility. I gave the figure for the occupancy as at the end of April this spring. Our peak load is in the winter, and possibly the figures for January would have shown a higher rate of occupancy. On the other hand, July and August will show less.
The matter of making use of any spare facilities in the hospitals, as I said, was studied very thoroughly. It was made the subject of a thorough investigation by officers of my department and of other departments. The possibility of making some of that accommodation available is rather remote. It must be understood that these hospitals, modern as they are, with the best personnel and equipment, still cannot handle certain patients. For example, they have not the facilities to look after children and certain other types of patients.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: They have plenty of beds.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: It would be very difficult, for example, to take care of women patients in these hospitals.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: They might admit other male patients.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend will permit me to continue. I will try to make my case clear and if he is not satisfied he can speak when I have completed my remarks. We have found it rather difficult to operate under the Department of Veterans Affairs such hospitals where the bulk of the patients would be veterans and where others would be civilians, so that we have evolved another scheme. I am glad the hon. member has mentioned this question because it will enable me to make a short statement in regard to some changes in the terms of our treatment regulations, to ensure that full use of the beds in our hospitals is made. We have come to the conclusion that we should amend the terms of the regulations so that veterans who wish to make use of the hospitals for treatment for non-pensionable disabilities can do so more easily than they can now. At the present time a veteran, if his income is below a certain ceiling, can obtain full treatment in the veterans hospitals free of charge. If his income is above that ceiling he is charged the daily rate which I mentioned a few moments ago in answer to a question by an hon. member. The department has for some time been studying a change in the regulations regarding assistance to veterans in the low income group for treatment of non-pensionable disability in our departmental hospitals. For some time it has been suggested that it would be desirable to get away from the principle of a fixed income ceiling and instead introduce the principle of a sliding scale so that while the lowest income group would pay nothing for treatment, those with a higher income would pay part of the cost of their treatment. The amount they would pay would be related to their income on a sliding scale.
The problem of working out such regulations was difficult but we eventually arrived at a definite plan which has been embodied in order in council P.C. 1954-849 which amends the terms of the present regulations.
Briefly the plan is that a single veteran whose income is less than $800, and a married veteran whose income is less than $1,200, will pay nothing for treatment. If their income is higher than that they will pay the cost of their treatment on a percentage basis up to one per cent of their income for each $100 income in excess of the amounts just stated. I might add that in computing income, allowance is made for dependent children and for wages lost owing to illness during the time
Supply-Veterans Affairs of hospitalization and convalescence. As an example of how this new plan works, if a married veteran with two children, earning $50 a week, had a severe illness and was hospitalized for two months, with a further one month convalescence, he would have to pay no more for his treatment in the hospital than $45. If he had to pay current expenses in a civil hospital, such an illness might very well leave him with a bill for $600 or more, apart from his own doctor's fees and extras.
It is expected that in many cases the veterans will be able to pay these charges for their treatment under this plan from prepaid health and hospital insurance.
Naturally, I cannot possibly explain all the details of this scheme without speaking at considerable length. I would say, however, that it is the intention to give adequate publicity to the new plan so that veterans who might benefit from it will be aware of their eligibility.
The department is confident that it will be possible to give treatment at a reduced cost proportionate to the veteran's ability to pay, and I might mention that many of the veterans who need this assistance were formerly ineligible under the previous regulations. We expect that with the implementation of these new regulations we will fill the empty beds which we may have in our hospitals at the present time.

this man's contention, and the pension board did change the category of his pension. It was increased considerably.
But if one has to go back to the pensions advocate who has considered the first diagnosis, you get the same reply all the time. Yet there may be cases where outside doctors should be consulted. They might take a different viewpoint, and their judgment might be correct.
Even if it is necessary to obtain the services of outside doctors I am sure the people of Canada want to know whether the veteran's contention is the correct one, or whether he is in error. We know there have been cases where assistance from outsiders has been most beneficial.

Mr. Chairman, the other night when we were discussing the first item in the minister's estimates there was considerable debate on the subject of war veterans allowances. At the adjournment hour I rose to speak, with a desire to follow the general line of discussion. However, we rose at that time and reported progress. Since that time I was informed that the minister was anxious to have the first item passed, and I agreed to that procedure in the light of the fact that there were other items on which this matter could be discussed.
I believe that what I have to say can properly be said under item 515. The matters of war veterans allowances, and the disappointment experienced because the terms of reference, in the recent parliamentary committee, were not broadened to include a discussion of war veterans allowances were gone into at considerable length, and I do not think I need take very much time in covering the matter again, or even in amplifying what has been said already.
There is not much left to say on the subject. The hon. member for Acadia, who represented this group in the war veterans committee, discussed the subject fully the other day, and paid particular attention to the permissive income feature. The hon. member for New Westminster followed in the debate and placed on record some further suggestions. The hon. member for Fraser Valley, also from this group, spoke on the subject. I rise at this time to support those members who have spoken on the matter and their desire that the war veterans allowance should be increased. I recognize that this is a matter of government policy. The previous speakers have not criticized the administration in any respect. In fact, all speakers have had the very highest regard for the administration itself, both the minister, who has a grasp of the entire situation in his department, and the officials who are under him in that department.
We are dealing with this matter as government policy, and it is government policy that we wish to criticize. When the resolution to set up the committee was on the order paper some months ago, I understand, a delegation from the dominion command waited on the Prime Minister and some of his cabinet, and requested that the matter of war veterans allowance should be included in the terms of reference of that committee.

Supply-Veterans Affairs I understand the Prime Minister was very frank with the delegation from the Legion command, and that is commendable. There is no use beating about the bush. If government policy is as it is, those responsible for pronouncing that policy might just as well come out and say so. The Prime Minister is to be commended on not hedging on the matter. I believe he told the command that government policy was such that they would not make an increase in the allowance; that to include it in the terms of reference would mean that they were giving some little hope that it might be done, and to give such hope would be misleading. Therefore the answer was no. He could not be any more direct than that, he could not be clearer, and he could not be any more honest than that. That was the right thing for him to do as far as his attitude or comment was concerned; but we criticize the answer he gave because we believe it was the wrong one. He should have been willing to permit the terms of reference to be widened with a view to recommendations being made, and the government should have been prepared to meet those recommendations.
We all have a great regard for the veterans. We know that when the veterans were called to the colours, either by conscription or through voluntary enlistment, they did not begin to weigh the consequences of their post-war life, and what they would get out of it afterwards. I wonder whether one might draw on his imagination. If a young chap went into a recruiting office and said: "I would like to join the forces, but there are a couple of questions I should like to ask before signing my name on the dotted line. Should I join the forces and play my part in the protection and preservation of democracy, if I offer my life for my country, what can I expect my country to do for me when I return?" If that recruiting officer had been able to look into the future he would have had to answer something like this:	"Well, I have it on the highest
authority that we will not do much of anything for you until you are in desperate need, and then we shall give you a subsistence allowance; but even then it will have to be under the means test." The young chap might have said:	"Since my people are
able to take care of me, what then?" The answer would be:	"Well, that is what they
should do, and if they take care of you and give you anything, then I am afraid we shall have to take that off your allowance." The young man might then reply:	"Suppose I
come back safely and I die and leave a widow, what is going to happen to her?" The

reply might be:	"Well, the same thing
would happen to her as would happen to you. If she is in need we will look after her, and if she is really in need we will see that she gets something, and of course that too will be under the means test." You can carry that illustration along as far as you like and then ask the question, would the young chap volunteer if he had been told the truth?

speechtext: I hope so.

I hope so, and I think he would, and I would not argue that case because I think anyone who wanted to volunteer had no thought of weighing the consequences of the post-war life. Nevertheless, when we look at it in that way the only conclusion we can come to is that any person who was called to the colours or enlisted, and went out and offered his life for his country, should be adequately cared for upon his return when the need arises.
On the basis of that we have a perfect right to say now that this matter of war veterans allowance should be continually studied. I know the minister will reply that they are continually studying the position of the war veterans in respect to allowances, but it should go further than that. The interest should be of such a character that a veterans committee of this house could sit down and discuss every possible veterans' problem and then come to the government with every possible recommendation. The government should weigh those recommendations and say: We will do all we can for those veterans. They should assume that that which is physically possible should be made financially possible.
I will not say anything else. I rose to support the previous speakers who have put on the record the desire of this group and others who have put on the record the desire of their various parties. Yesterday on the orders of the day the Prime Minister was asked if he would still consider the matter. He gave the answer as a definite no. Well, we can conclude that at this session nothing is to be done. Might I urge the government to take this matter under very serious advisement during the next few months, and at the commencement of the next session come down with a program of allowances that we shall indeed be proud of. Might I urge the government to do that? It would be one of the finest things that happened in this session if the minister could rise before the items are concluded and say: we expect to do something within the next session of parliament.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
I am sure the minister will receive some satisfaction from the fact that

there has not been any criticism of the administration of this important department of government. Most of the discussion has been about this controversial question which we are now discussing. Since coming back to parliament in 1953 I have had very few complaints from the various Legion branches in my constituency. Apparently there is quite a marked improvement over conditions of some years ago. I think that members in all sections of the house have made their remarks in the hope that the minister might have a larger share of the total national budget for his particular department.
During the early years of the war we had a visit from the then minister of finance in New Zealand, and I have never forgotten the policy of the New Zealand government as he outlined it to us then. He said they were going to do everything in their power to see that those who went to war would not be worse off than if they remained at home. Secondly, that no one who remained at home would be better off at the end of the war because he remained at home.
The present Minister of National Defence was a private member then, as I was, and I was interested to hear him speaking in Montreal shortly after he became Minister of National Defence and he pointed out that the goal of this government was exactly the policy outlined by Mr. Nash.
However, I do not feel that the government of Canada has dealt as generously with the Minister of Veterans Affairs as with his colleague the Minister of National Defence. I followed the minister very closely the other night, and he stated that the proposal made by the Legion would increase our liabilities by about $27 million which would be an increase of about 95 per cent. I think we must ask ourselves whether the Canadian economy will stand an additional burden of $27 million to discharge our responsibilities for war veterans allowances. I realize it is easy for members in opposition groups to recommend increased expenditure all along the line. But I think it should be stated that the Canadian Legion is a non-partisan organization and it is comprised of honest, stable citizens who do not recommend expenditures which are unreasonable.
I have in my hand a report of the Department of Defence Production for the year 1953 and I find that this department points out that up to the end of 1953 certificates had been issued covering some $665 million of capital investment in facilities for the production of both basic materials and defence supplies, and thereby allowing additional benefits by way of income tax write-offs amounting to $277 million. It adds that
Supply-Veterans Affairs the Canadian government defence procurement expenditures during the year totalled $1,174 million, slightly up from the amount for the previous year.
Now, no hon. member of parliament has criticized this expenditure. But I think that if we are going to spend $2,000 million for defence purposes it must be agreed that Canada must discharge its responsibilties to the veterans of world wars I and II and the Korean war.
I found myself in a position where I was too young for the first war and too old for the second war, and so I think I can say that those of us who remained at home found ourselves in the most prosperous period in Canadian history. I believe at this stage that to increase compensation to veterans to the extent of $27 million is not going to place an unreasonable drain on the Canadian economy.
Following the line of the remarks made by the hon. member for Macleod, I think that our treatment of soldier settlers after the first world war is not a performance of which we can be especially proud. I remember a delegation coming to Ottawa during the war years trying to get legislation to relieve them of their farm indebtedness. These men stated they did not think they would be a good recruiting team to go across Canada to outline what their experience had been farming in Canada after they had "made the world safe for democracy". I remember one time I found myself in a veterans affairs office making representations on behalf of the widow of a very close friend of mine. This chap was the principal of a school and he enlisted and gave his life for his country while in the service of the air force in Egypt. At that time his widow found her income drastically reduced. She had a young son to support and she found it necessary to seek assistance to go to business college to supplement her income. The veterans affairs officer was very sympathetic and he told her that if she had lost her husband during the first war the pension would have been much less. I shall never forget her reply. She said: "If my husband had remained as principal of the school I would not now be in a position where my income was cut so drastically that I could not support the young lad and give him the kind of education he would have had if his father had remained at home". I do not think anyone would try to defend the position in which that widow found herself, because she is now very much worse off because her husband gave his life for his country.
So, Mr. Chairman, I would like to suggest to the Minister of Veterans Affairs that he

-of making a statement on this important subject. Looking at the minister's statement, I find there are many points which are helpful and enlightening regarding the question of war veterans allowance. My observation, however, is that it is unfortunate that such a statement was not made before the special committee which recently concluded its deliberations. Special committees are called together for the purpose of dealing with matters which are more or less contentious, and I do not think any 

hon. member will take exception to the statement that the subject of war veterans allowance is a rather contentious one at the present time. It is not possible to come to the close grips necessary in any discussion that arises out of the minister's statement to the committee of the whole on Thursday last. After my experience while sitting in the committee, I came away from the committee with a feeling of frustration with regard to this subject of war veterans allowance. Unfortunately the elucidation given by the minister has not dissipated that feeling because I feel certain that there is much more to be said on this subject that has received such great emphasis during the past three or four years by the veterans of this country and by those who are interested in veterans' welfare.
One point I should like to make particularly is the interpretation given by the minister with regard to the purpose served by the implementation of the war veterans allowance legislation back in the year 1930, I believe it was. In his statement, as reported at pages 6194 and 6195 of Hansardhe emphasized that it was legislation to provide for a premature old age pension at age 60; that is, it was considered that veterans, as the result of their war service, had aged prematurely by at least 10 years. Throughout the minister's statement he emphasized the continuing connection between war veterans allowance and the principle of old age payments.
It is true that he points out that the bounds of the war veterans allowance have enlarged considerably since the legislation was originally introduced, but in the argument supporting the government's present stand on the matter he comes back repeatedly to the comparison between war veterans allowance and old age pension legislation. It seems to me that in the application of the war veterans allowance legislation down through the years it has been expanded to include marginal disability cases as well as those who come under the terms of premature ageing. In many cases of disability that show up years after the veteran has been discharged and has returned to his civilian pursuits, it is almost impossible to rule whether the disability is the result of war service. This statement is particularly true in the case of functional or hysterical disorders. During the sitting of the committee I attempted to discuss this matter and I found that there was much hazy thinking on the matter of disabilities other than direct physical disabilities. Since the committee rose I have been checking the Pension Act, and I have discovered that section 32

of that act deals specifically with these problems in subsections 2, 3 and 4. Subsection 2 reads as follows:
(2)	When in the opinion of a medical neurological expert an applicant for pension or a pensioner has a disability that is purely functional or hysterical no pension shall be paid, but such member of the forces shall immediately be referred to a neurological centre for treatment.
Then in subsection 3 the act goes on to enlarge further on the point. Subsection 3 reads as follows:
(3)	In cases in which the functional or hysterical disability disappears as the result of treatment the commission may, in its discretion, award a gratuity in final payment not exceeding five hundred dollars but no pension shall be paid.
Then subsection 4 reads as follows:
(4)	When as the result of treatment the functional or hysterical disability has not disappeared a pension shall be awarded in accordance with the extent of the disability, if the applicant or pensioner has not unreasonably refused to accept or continue treatment.
In some of the cases which have become eligible for war veterans allowance and with which I have come in contact, I would come to the conclusion that they are victims of hysterical or functional disorders or, as the psychologists put it, they are victims of neurotic difficulties. It seems to me that because of the vague handling of the problem in the Pension Act the interpretation of the War Veterans Allowance Act in practice has been extended to cover this particular problem group. That being so, I think the terms of the act go far beyond the comparison that has been drawn between war veterans allowance and old age pension. In view of this conclusion, I maintain that the demands which have been put forward for several years now by the Legion are not unreasonable. If we literally interpret the war veterans allowance as being comparable with the old age pension and all veterans automatically become eligible at 60, resulting in an expenditure of some $27 million, under the proposed increases as the minister indicated in his statement the other evening, perhaps it would be necessary to review the interpretation of the legislation and to draw the lines more clearly so that adequate payment might be made to those marginal disability cases to which I have referred, particularly those suffering from functional or hysterical disability.
Unfortunately, discussion of this subject in the committee of the whole does not provide the opportunity to go into the detailed discussion that would have been possible had the minister made his statement in the special committee and had we been able to have a thorough give-and-take discussion there on this important matter.

speechtext:
It is unfortunate, Mr. Chairman, that we cannot devote more time to a department as important as the Department of National Health and Welfare. In view of the large amount of money expended by this department, it would be impossible and futile, within the space of four or five hours in an afternoon, to attempt to investigate the financial end of the department's operations. It is true that a large proportion of the money expended by the department is statutory. I refer to the money expended on old age pensions, the new disability pensions and family allowances. These are purely statutory, and if there were any question about them it would be as to the adequacy of the administration.
Therefore I believe that the average member, in going over the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, simply takes the attitude that money spent for health is money well spent and leaves it to the minister and his officials to carry out this work. With an important subject of this kind it would be better if we could have a committee so that we might be able to spend a longer time in examining these estimates. There is nothing so important as national health and welfare, and it would be most helpful if we could spend further time not only in investigating the financial aspect but in making recommendations to the minister. I am sure the minister would be glad to hear them, and we would also be able to hear more from the minister on points of interest involved in the consideration of his estimates.
There is one thing that is always very important in the consideration of these estimates, the investigation and inquiry into the causes of mortality in the dominion in the last year. These do not seem to change very much from year to year. Some changes are taking place with new types of treatment, but we note that the same old enemies are at the top of the list. I refer to cancer, heart disease and the so-called vascular diseases. Changes are taking place with respect to them, and we cannot always trust statistics to show the true picture because people are living longer and it is only natural in their old age they should fall prey to some form of disease. There has to be something that carries them away.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Therefore while the statistics on cancer may seem to indicate that its incidence is greater, it is only natural that people living to an old age will develop this disease or others, particularly heart disease. With reference to heart disease, I should like to emphasize the necessity for some form of accelerated research into the many causes of sudden death by coronary disease not only in Canada but in other countries. Research is being conducted but there is a need for acceleration of the investigation of something that is really becoming a problem. Frequently our attention is directed to the fact that some person has passed away with coronary disease. In the newspapers we only see the names of people whose passing has drawn the attention of reporters. We know that public men are passing away early in life from coronary disease, and I should like to suggest to the minister that every dollar that can be spent on accelerated research into the cause of death from coronary disease should be spent because it is becoming a problem.
In looking over the causes of death in the Dominion of Canada, I was struck by the large number of deaths from accidents. It may be that part of what I am going to say was discussed at the time of the consideration of amendments to the Criminal Code. I am referring to traffic accidents, but in view of the fact that accidental deaths are now the fourth cause of death in Canada I think it well that something should be placed on the record in this regard. I do so for the reason that I believe that consideration of this matter in the federal parliament on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare may add some impetus to doing something about it.
I wish to place on the record certain statistics which I think are rather frightening. I also wish to read a short extract from that highly reputable magazine, The Canadian Doctor. It is true that some 5,000 accidents occur through other causes, but industry is striving very hard to avoid accidents. Organizations like the workmen's compensation boards are making inquiries into the causes of accidents in industry and are doing everything possible to cut down the mortality and injury rates. However, traffic accidents seem to be increasing. Two days ago the hon. member for Oxford asked one of the ministers for statistics regarding traffic accidents. The minister did not have them available, and I do not think they are issued by the dominion bureau of statistics. Therefore, with the permission of the committee, I am going to read a short article from The Canadian Doctor.
The article was written by a highly reputable medical practitioner, Dr. Harold Elliott, who is a prominent Montreal neurosurgeon, and I note that the article commences with a quotation from certain remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I do not know where he made these remarks. Possibly it was in the course of some address that he delivered, but I must say that I agree with him. It was a very suitable introduction to the short article on the unenviable record of the Dominion of Canada. In the minister's statement I find these words:
In the past fifty years our general mortality rate has been reduced by one-third, placing Canada fourth among the nations of the world.
This is the important sentence.
Were it not for the increasing toll taken by accidents, our general mortality rate would be even better.
Accidents, as I said, are the fourth ranking cause of death in this country. I wish to read the article, and I will ask the permission of the house to place the statistical records on Hansard. The article reads as follows:
Last May in The Canadian Doctor Dr. Harold Elliott, prominent Montreal neurosurgeon, attempted to bring home to Canadian medical men in general the appalling and steadily mounting mortality rate from automobile accidents and stir them, as dedicated to the preservation of life, to a sense of responsibility for concerted action which would reduce this. As pointed out by him, a total of 2,500 automobile passengers killed and approximately 54,000 injured in 1952 ranked this as one of the leading causes of death and maiming in the dominion. One is not surprised at the statement of the world health organization, made after the first international study of transport mortality covering fifteen countries, that "mortality from transport accidents represents one of the most important causes of death at certain ages" but it is distressing to find that Canada has almost the worst and least enviable record in this regard.
Twenty-two types of transport accidents are analysed in the W.H.O. study. The motor vehicle comes far ahead of all other means of transport as a cause of death. Far lower in the statistical scale are railway accidents, followed by road accidents caused by non-motor vehicles, and water transport accidents. Aircraft accidents appear at the bottom of the list and mostly affect personnel in military aircraft.
A comparison between the death rate caused by transport accidents and that resulting from disease shows that in a number of countries transport accidents rank with tuberculosis as a killer, especially of men; they are far more dangerous than many diseases such as nephritis, diabetes, and sometimes influenza. And transport accidents kill more men than women.
But it is among the young, where the general death rate is naturally low, that traffic is the number one killer. In certain countries one fourth, one third, or even more young people who die between the ages of 15 and 24 are killed in transport accidents. In this age group males are more likely to be killed than females, the proportion reaching as high as five to one.
What it is wished to emphasize here is Canada's unenviable record internationally in this regard. Those who were appalled at the Canadian situation

as presented by Dr. Elliott must be further shocked to learn that both as regards general transport deaths and deaths from this cause in the age group 15 to 24 Canada has one of the worst records in the world. It should prove further disturbing to doctors and bolster the argument they concertedly make themselves responsible for doing something about it.
I am going to place these tables before the house. The first table shows the proportion of deaths due to all transport accidents compared with general mortality, from all causes, in percentage. Supply-Health and Welfare It may seem unusual to some people that I have brought this matter before the house during consideration of the estimates of national health and welfare. I know that the minister has not any responsibility with regard to these casualties, but on the other hand we are considering the dominion estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare and this cause of death is fourth in the list of mortality rates. In the matter of health and welfare, I have always been rather jealous of the position of the provinces. The control of health matters is within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but sometimes across the country a misunderstanding seems to arise as to who is doing the greatest work in that connection. Sometimes, in my jealousy over the position of the provinces, I feel that the federal government is taking credit for some of the things the provincial governments are doing.
I should like to put on the record the position with regard to hospital grants. Many times during the last few years I have mentioned the amount of money that the provinces are spending. The federal government does not match the total amount of money spent by the provincial government. It is true the federal government gives matching grants for hospital construction, but in connection with the work done in my own province the provincial government spends $2.57 for every dollar spent by the federal government, that is so far as 1953 is concerned. The federal government does contribute thousands of dollars for hospitals, but does not contribute towards the maintenance of the hospitals. The Ontario government, for instance, makes a grant of $8,500 for beds in mental institutions, but the federal government only contributes $1,500 towards that work.
It is true the federal government does contribute money towards mental health, but I want to place on the record the fact that the provinces are still doing a tremendous job in the advancement of health projects.
While I am speaking about this matter of the work done in the provinces in relation to the work done by the dominion, I wish to bring before the house one item which I feel
6296	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare should have consideration from this committee. I refer to the question of the growing number of mental cases in this country.
I was struck by a statement that came from the dominion bureau of statistics indicating that patients in mental hospitals and psychiatric units outnumber all other patients in hospitals by more than 10 per cent. At the end of 1952-and that is the last date for which the complete figures were available- there were 61,925 patients in mental hospitals, while the number of all other patients in public hospitals was 54,284. I shall repeat those figures: 61,925 mental patients, and all other patients in hospitals numbering 54,284.
This brings us to the question of the shortage of beds in mental institutions, and the difficulty of obtaining treatment for cases in those institutions of those we have found it necessary to send there. While I am not in active practice at the present time, people still come to me and ask me if I can do anything to help get a patient into a mental hospital, because the waiting period is so long.
It is difficult to treat a mental case in a private home, but sometimes these patients have to wait some considerable time before beds are found available. If we are going to deal with this question, and if we keep in mind that 10 per cent of mental cases over all other types of cases in hospitals, then we have to do a great deal, and possibly something more than we are doing at the present time. A great deal of good could be accomplished by the extension of mental health units. I note-and I agree with the procedure-that the federal government is giving grants for that sort of thing. But we have to go much farther. While the provinces with the larger populations are making beds available, and trying to accommodate these people as rapidly as they can, one wonders if it would not be good policy to have smaller hospitals, or branches of psychiatric units attached to our larger hospitals. Thereby something could be done by way of early treatment.
It is known at the present time that there is more to the treatment of mental cases than just the matter of custodial care. An increasing percentage of these people are coming out of the hospitals in a cured condition. If we could have smaller psychiatric units attached to our larger hospitals there would be a chance to treat these cases earlier, so as to try to bring the disease under control. A great deal of work could be done among younger people in the mental health units.
I am aware that the government in my province has been working on this scheme,


and has been doing good work in treating the cases early and attempting to make cures.
I now go back to the information given out by the dominion bureau of statistics regarding mental disease. Perhaps I might quote from a newspaper article based on a statement made by the bureau of statistics, as follows:
Advances in combating infectious diseases in prolonging life expectancy, and in the general improvement in physical health have not been matched by comparable reductions in the incidence of mental disorders. Indeed, the successful control of a number of deadly diseases has served rather to accentuate the seriousness of mental illness as the cause of much suffering and unhappiness, and from another viewpoint, a great wastage of our human resources.
I hope that in Canada we can institute a program. While I realize that health is within the jurisdiction of the provinces, I believe we can do something to combat a condition in which, as I repeat, the number of patients in mental hospitals is 10 per cent higher than the number of admissions to ordinary hospitals
I am not going to talk about the incidence of some of the diseases we have covered in years gone by. As I said in the beginning, the percentages per population are probably getting better. In the past I have criticized our rate of infant mortality as compared with that in other countries. I must say however that this rate is improving; and I give credit to the research done on the subject. Advances in forms of treatment as well as new drugs have helped a great deal.
At this time I should like to pay tribute to the people who are working on this problem. I refer particularly to the general practitioners who are meeting the problem of treating these children, in infancy, and at early ages. I think much of the progress we are now making in the matter of infant mortality is due to those practitioners, and we can congratulate them upon the work they are doing. But last year I was alarmed, as I have no doubt were also the minister and the department, by the growing incidence in the outbreaks of poliomyelitis or infantile paralysis. I have here the record of poliomyelitis in Canada for 1953. The information is given by provinces, and I note two things about it. First of all, the greater number of cases occurred in July, August, September and October, and even into November, and that they occurred in the western provinces.
We have not yet got the answer to poliomyelitis, but some wonderful research is being done throughout the world, and particularly in Canada. I refer to that being done at the Connaught laboratories in an attempt to prepare something that will cope

with this disease. But, so tar as cure is concerned, we must go back to the therapeutic measures which have been instituted to try to stop the horrible crippling that occurs.
In this connection I would refer again to the work being done in Ontario. I would call the attention of hon. members to the excellent results obtained when Ontario instituted a program under which every case of poliomyelitis or infantile paralysis becomes a ward of the province for treatment purposes. From the time a case is diagnosed, the province takes over all the treatment. Looking back on the results obtained years ago, before this program was instituted, I find it amazing to note some of the recoveries that have been made. Not only is it important that these young people should be spared the crippling effects of this disease, but it is important from the standpoint of the state.
Only a few days ago we were discussing a bill with respect to disability. We were proud and pleased to vote money to disabled persons by way of pensions. But I suggest that the program which has been instituted in Ontario, to which I have just made reference, could be carried out in all the provinces of Canada. So far as can be done by way of treatment, it would go a long way toward clearing up the crippling effects of this disease.
I should like now to say a few words with regard to hospitals. The financing and building of new hospitals requires a great deal of money. Sometimes it is difficult for the public to understand why there is this constant demand for more beds, more accommodation. But I am going to place before the committee some of the statistics from my own province so that hon. members may have some of the facts in connection with hospitalization. It is not generally understood why there is such a demand, but certain facts stand out. Our population is not static. Every year there is an increase in population and that increase means that we must have more hospital accommodation, more hospitals for treatment of that increased population.
I should like to point out that advances in medical science, new forms of treatment, have made it imperative that these people be treated in hospital. That means that hospitals that were once adequate in size must be enlarged, and for those rapidly growing communities hospitals must be provided. It requires a great deal more money now to construct new buildings than it did years ago. The costs have risen very sharply. The assistance from the federal government and the provincial government constitutes really only a small part of the actual cost of the 83276-398J
Supply-Health and Welfare hospital facilities. The citizens themselves and the municipalities have to share in the cost of providing hospital services for their own communities.
What is the position of the municipalities? It is true that a certain amount of money will be raised for this purpose by appeals to the public. On the other hand, the municipalities find it very difficult to finance the building of new hospitals or the expansion of existing hospitals, and very often the maintenance of older existing hospitals.
In the consideration this morning of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs certain figures were placed on the record regarding the cost of hospitalization. I take these figures from the Ontario records. The average length of stay in hospitals now is shorter than it formerly was. It is 9-23 days; but the average cost of a patient in a hospital per day to provide for his treatment is $12.58-these figures refer to the year 1952 -as opposed to $11.54 per day in 1951. There is an increase of $1.04 within one year. Out of this amount-and I am referring to Ontario; I am not acquainted with the records of the other provinces, but I think the comparison will be practically the same in all of them- of $12.58 per patient per day, the patient pays only $8.83. The difference has to be made up by grants from the various governments, federal, provincial or municipal, or from another level, namely, donations from the people who are interested in hospitals.
Something further is happening; more people are going to the hospitals because it is increasingly difficult to get help in the home or to get nurses. And, as I said, much of this treatment that is now given has to be given in hospital. We have arrived at the stage where practically 90 per cent of the babies are born in hospitals. The expenses have gone up. At the end of 1952 there were 9,855 more employees on hospital staffs than in 1947. In the matter of wages and salaries, they have increased. I often hear people say: why are hospitals costing so much? Why this constant appeal to the public? Since 1941 wages and salaries have gone up 150 per cent. Not only that, but food costs have gone up 200 per cent, and the hospital cost for drugs and medical supplies rose in that period of not quite ten years by 114 per cent. Therefore one can understand quite readily, when I make this appeal for more money for the hospitals, that there is a reason, and these figures should be placed on the record so that people can understand why hospital costs have gone up.
I now come to the question of nursing staffs and nurses in Canada. I hear the statement
6298	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare made that we generally suffer from a shortage of some 10,000 nurses in Canada, although I know somebody said that the distribution was at fault. It is difficult, but it is costing the hospitals something to give nurses an education. Again 1 turn to the records of Ontario, which has about 5,000 nurses in training at all times. But so far as the hospitals are concerned, it represents an expenditure of $1,500,000 on education, for which those hospitals receive no educational grants. The position of the hospitals is increasingly difficult, and any person who has had any experience on the board of a hospital trying to finance a hospital and keep out of the red will know it is a very difficult position. Many of the municipalities are very much worried in trying to maintain hospitals, although the demand for more hospitals and more hospital beds is constantly before us.
I am not going to speak on the matter of the statistics of this department any further, sir, but at this time I wish to bring before the committee a few remarks on health insurance. I am going to ask the minister one question only when we come to the item on health insurance studies, and that is this. What is the minister doing and what has been accomplished? Will the minister give us a full statement on the studies that are being made? I bring this question of health insurance before the committee because in the past statements have been made in regard to a vote that was taken here in December, 1953, on the amendment to the speech from the throne that was introduced by the C.C.F. party. I have found a certain amount of propaganda going out that the Conservative party voted against health insurance. I thought I explained to the house at that time that we voted against socialized medicine. I made it very clear at that time-
