speechtext: What is the difference?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: There is a large difference.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Explain it to us.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
I will, shortly. I made it clear at that time in the latter part of my speech that every party in this house is committed to health insurance. I admit, sir, that any form will produce and do some good, but we are committed to a form of contributory insurance. It is not sufficient to say that every form is the same. There is a great deal of difference in them, and the more you study them, the more do those differences become apparent. In the first place, one must realize that health is within the jurisdiction of the provinces. One cannot get around that. The second thing is that if you are going to make health insurance succeed at any time, one of the most important


things to remember is the matter of doctor-patient relationship. That must be preserved, no matter what happens. No health insurance scheme can be effective unless the doctor-patient relationship is preserved. The views of the doctor on this matter are very important. I say that not because I belong to that profession; but I hold that we must receive their help, their co-operation, their good will and their agreement before any form of health insurance can be a success. Our idea of health insurance is not state medicine. We believe in a minimum of controls, not a maximum.
We want this to be a free form, a free plan. I do pay tribute to the many forms of free insurance at the present time-Blue Cross, and some of the forms that have been instituted by the doctors themselves. They are doing marvellous work in this country. Therefore those facts become very apparent in the consideration of that question; but there are certain facts regarding state medicine, and I wish to place on the record the views of a very important and outstanding man from England, Dr. Reginald Hale-White, who addressed the Canadian Medical Association at its convention last week. I quote from a dispatch from Vancouver regarding a speech he made out there:
Dr. Reginald Hale-White of London says socialized medicine in Britain leaves "much to be desired, because it is not giving the general public its full worth."
And remember, sir, I stated that any plan will do a certain amount of good, but we in Canada are looking for the best plan. I continue with Dr. Hale-White's statement:
The doctor, on the council of the British Medical Association, is representing the BMA at the Canadian Medical Association convention here.
The service in England, he said, "is costing the public $1,400 million a year.
"It is not at all what the politicians said it would be," he said, "and it should have been introduced gradually, instead of with a bang, as it was.
Dr Hale-White listed four complaints against the medical scheme, which has been in effect since
1948.
They were:	, . .	..
1 The introduction of the scheme led to the belittling of the general practitioner, because the government stressed that the public would have access to the best specialists under socialized
medicine.	..	, .	. .
2. People began bothering the doctors and hospitals with trivial matters.
3.	The time a doctor could give his patients was boiinhalleneed by paper work necessary under
me swiciuc.
4.	Hospitals became cluttered with cases that should have been handled by general practitioners but were not because of lack of time.
The doctor, who is leaving Friday for a cross-Canada tour and then home, warned that these are some of the things that should be watched under any national or provincial hospital insurance plan in Canada.

I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that this party is in favour of health insurance. We are opposed to state medicine. We believe a contributory plan could be introduced which would cover the situation without having state medicine in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all members of the house will agree that we have come this afternoon to a discussion of one of the most important functions of government. That applies to the work being done by the federal Department of National Health and Welfare. It also applies to the work being done by the various provincial departments of health and also the great amount of work being done at the municipal level. I think also of the great deal of work in the field of health care that is done by the school boards and school districts of this country.
As I say, we feel that this is one of the most important functions of government at all levels of government in Canada. I do not want anyone to infer from what I have just said that despite its importance there has been no discussion of health and welfare matters at this session. I do not rise to make the charge that it has been left to the dying days of this session. That would certainly be inappropriate for a department and a function of government which is so important, and we made sure that these matters were discussed all through the session.
The fact is that we have had quite a number of discussions during the course of this session on matters that come within the purview of this department. The hon. member for Lanark referred a few moments ago to the amendment which was moved by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, which was the subject of discussion during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The words in question were these:
We further represent that this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation.
In addition, we have had discussions spread through the session on a number of other matters that come under this department. We have had two or three discussions on the subject of old age pensions, including both old age assistance and old age security. Indeed, on May 31 there was before the house in my name an amendment to the motion to go into ways and means dealing with old age assistance, old age security, and blind pensions. We have also had a discussion on the question of family allowances which was
Supply-Health and Welfare precipitated by a private member's motion presented to the house by my deskmate, the hon. member for Assiniboia.
As the hon. member for Lanark pointed out, we have also had a discussion on disability allowances arising out of the legislation which the Minister of National Health and Welfare at last introduced in connection with that matter. In addition to these formal debates, Mr. Chairman, there have been repeated questions throughout the session on matters relating to health and welfare which bear witness to the tremendous importance of this phase of government.
I think too of the meetings that have been held during the course of the session by the voluntary committee on health to which both senators and members of this house belong and at which we have had some very interesting lectures, including one a short while ago on the very important question of poliomyelitis.
I think it is true to say, Mr. Chairman, that parliament generally has been conscious throughout this session of the importance of the work of this department. I believe in fact that the department of health and welfare includes amongst its many divisions one division which is one of the oldest functions of government. I refer to the division which deals with food and drugs. In other words, it was recognized quite early in the history of this country that one of the jobs that had to be done by the federal government was that of taking protective or preventive measures for the health of the Canadian people. We have gone a long way since those early days when the extent of the responsibility for health was confined to that negative or preventive field covered by the protection of food and drugs. We have come to recognize that with an economy such as ours, and with the growing extent to which our society is one in which we are members one of another, it is our responsibility to provide for the health and well-being of the members of the community to the very limit of our capacity.
I welcome, as do all hon. members of this group, and as do all hon. members of the house, the progress we have made in that direction even though we might spend most of the time when we talk of these matters emphasizing the distance we have yet to travel. But welcome though we may the progress that has been made in the past, we feel that there is not really time enough to sit around rejoicing in that progress when there is so much yet to be done.
Having said a few things about the department in perhaps a little more complimentary
6300	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare vein than that in which I am usually known to indulge, as the minister will confirm, I might add that we feel a great deal of good has been accomplished in the field of health and welfare, particularly since health and welfare was set up as a department by itself. It took a few years after the original organization of this new department for it to get into its stride, and such moves as it has made were made we think in response to pressures put upon the government from this house and in response to the pressure of public opinion.
Perhaps the most significant forward step in the field of health taken by the department is that which was taken in May, 1948, when the health grants program was launched. I will not allow the minister to forget that the prime minister of that day declared on that occasion that the health grants program was to be the basis for a nation-wide program of health insurance. I hope the day is not too far off when there will be built the superstructure for which that foundation was laid. Under that health grants program a great deal of assistance has been given in the construction of hospitals. Let us give credit to all those to whom it is due in that connection. Let us give credit to the federal government for the appropriation of federal public money for this purpose. But let us give credit also to provincial governments and to all others who have contributed toward increasing the number of hospital beds in this country.
In addition to the building of hospitals that has been done under the health grants program, there were other grants-there are a good many of them now-such as the crippled children's grant, the grant for the combating of cancer, the grant with respect to mental diseases and so on. We think too of the tremendous amount of research that is being done under the various grants. Some of it is done directly by the department and some of it involves money being made available to institutes or to organizations able to carry on research in the fields of cancer, poliomyelitis, multiple sclerosis or others of these diseases which, even to our medical people, are still a mystery and the solution to which would mean so much to the health of our people. We welcome the work that is being done under the health grants program; but, as I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will not think that I am going to stop there. I shall continue to remind him of what Mr. Mackenzie King said, namely that one of the reasons for initiating this health grants program was so as to lay the foundation for a nation-wide program of health insurance.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for those kind words.

I hope the minister will express that appreciation in a practical way by fighting still harder within the cabinet of which he is a member for the right to introduce at an early date a nation-wide health insurance program.
I also want to say, Mr. Chairman, that one of the other forward steps that was taken by this department during the last few years was that which was taken when the means test was removed from the old age pension at least at age 70 and when we got started on a new concept of old age security as a right belonging to the people of this country rather than as a matter of charity. I am not going to take the time to repeat the speeches I have made on that question times without number in this chamber. I just want to add to my appreciation of what was done by saying that we want that principle, the principle that social security is a right, to be extended still further. As I indicated when I moved an amendment to the motion to go into ways and means on May 31, we believe that the amount of the old age pension should now be increased to not less than $60 a month, and we feel that the means test should be removed at age 65. We indicated also, with respect to that other forward step, namely the disability pension, that it too should be raised to the figure of $60 a month.
In connection with the progress that we made a few years ago with regard to our old age security legislation, and recalling the work of our committee which recommended the abolition of the means test, may I take a moment to refer in passing to a couple of items that I noticed in the press a short while ago. I may be getting off base a bit but it is late in the session, so why not? I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I shall never forget the real assistance that we had in our committee on old age security from one of the present minister's deputies. I refer to the deputy minister of welfare, Dr. George F. Davidson. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is very ably assisted by two deputy ministers, namely Dr. George F. Davidson as deputy minister of welfare and Dr. G. D. W. Cameron as deputy minister of health.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: I knew the minister would agree with me.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: The hon. member may be accused of looking for a seat in the Senate; he had better be careful.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Not I. It is only proof of the importance of the work of this department that it has to have two deputy ministers. What I saw in the paper which disturbed me a bit was a rumour that we might lose Dr. Davidson from the Department of National Health and Welfare. There is no doubt that he could do a good job in the position to which it was rumoured he might move, but I must say I would be sorry if we lost him from this important Department of National Health and Welfare. However, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not able to hold Dr. Davidson against the inducements or blandishments that may be offered to him by one of his colleagues, I was also interested in noting in the press the rumour-one of those informed guesses, as it were-that if that happened the Prime Minister might then have the opportunity to appoint the first woman to become a deputy minister under this government. I am glad that she is within the sound of my voice and knows that if that happens it would have my approval. From the applause of other members I gather that the appointment of Miss Olive Waters as deputy minister of welfare would be approved generally in the House of Commons.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Are there any other appointments?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Not today. Perhaps that is enough along that line, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of National Health and Welfare may wonder whether I am not feeling well, having got this far in my speech without having something critical to say. I now come to that point. I have already indicated that we feel that greater effort should be made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to persuade his colleagues that the time has come for increasing the amounts paid under various social security acts. I refer to old age pensions, blindness pensions and disability allowances. However, Mr. Chairman, the gap in our social security program which is the most serious of all-the one which I regret has not yet been filled-is that of national health insurance. As I have said already, Mr. King made it clear in May, 1948, that that was the purpose of the health grants program, namely to lay a foundation for nation-wide health insurance. Someone may say: That was only six years ago; what is your hurry? The minister knows that I must remind him again that national health insurance was first put into the Liberal platform in 1919. That was 35 years ago.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: And it is still there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH

The hon. member for Fort William says that it is still there. I suggest
Supply-Health and Welfare to the hon. member for Fort William and to members generally on the other side of the chamber that the time has come to take that plank out of the Liberal platform and put it on the statute books of Canada. Thirty-five years is a long time ago, Mr. Chairman. I can remember back that far but I cannot remember much farther back.
I submit that the time has come for definite action on this question. As a matter of fact, a new generation of Canadians-indeed a new generation of Liberals-has grown up which is now getting interested in this question. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of Monday, May 31, 1954. The heading is "National Insurance Advocated". The first paragraph reads as follows:
Ottawa, May 30-CP-Canada's young Liberals Saturday urged the government to implement a national contributory health insurance plan in co-operation with the provinces.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fort William, one of the young Liberals over there, says "hear, hear". I am glad to know that there is still support in the Liberal ranks for this plank of national health insurance. The hon. member for Lanark says he is going to ask one question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare when we get down to that item. I ask him the same question. What are you doing about this? When are we going to get national health insurance? Surely the minister and the government generally are not going to argue that they have got to wait any longer to ascertain public opinion in connection with this matter. Surely they must know that people all over Canada today are conscious of the heavy costs of medical expenses. They are conscious of how these expenses bear down on them when they have to be met. They are conscious of the fact that a great many people do not have the medical or hospital care which they should have because of the heavy cost.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has had some part to play in having sickness surveys made, and I have been interested in some of the facts that have been brought out by these surveys. For example, I hold in my hand a portion of the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin for September 21, 1953, which shows several breakdowns of a sickness survey, the results of which had been announced at that time, and this one interested me in particular. Out of 1,322,000 family units with incomes less than $1,500 nearly one-fifth, 19-8 per cent, spent nothing on health care compared with 7-7 per cent of 1,864,000 with incomes of $1,500 to $2,299, 4-3 per cent of 833,000 with
6302	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare incomes of $3,000 to $4,999 and 3 per cent of 271,000 with incomes of $5,000 or more.
May I pick out two figures there to make a comparison which drives home the point I have in mind. The point is that of those family units whose incomes are $1,500 a year or less nearly 20 per cent have spent nothing in the whole year on health care, but when you take those with $5,000 a year or more there are only 3 per cent who spent nothing on health care.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he not think that the young Liberals showed good sense when they supported national health insurance in cooperation with the provinces instead of the dominion going it alone?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: As a matter of fact that was the gist of the amendment which my leader moved last November 16. It asked for a nation-wide health insurance program with provision for provincial participation. That appears to be what the young Liberals supported in their motion the other day, but the hon. member for Fort William voted against it when we moved it in the house last year.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Want of confidence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
There is the old dodge, want of confidence. We think that the health of the people is more important than the survival of any particular government. I was pointing out that of those family units whose income is $1,500 a year or less nearly 20 per cent spent nothing on health care whereas of those whose incomes were $5,000 a year or more only 3 per cent got through the year without spending anything on health care. We all know, Mr. Chairman, that it stands to reason that the people with low incomes are not going to be healthier than the people with higher incomes. The reverse is the case. What it means is simply this, that the people with low incomes cannot afford the health care that they so sorely need.
Surely it has been recognized by everyone, young Liberals and old and Canadians generally, that the only solution to the heavy cost of adequate medical care is to put it on an over-all or universal basis. We have had that brought out in other ways during the course of this session. I am not going to revive the debate we had a few days ago on a form of life insurance when the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant both drove home the point, and did it very well, that the only way you could make sure that an entire group would have a certain amount of insurance protection was to put it on an over-all or universal basis.


They both said that that was the only way to make sure they would all have it. They said it was the only way to make sure that the cost of it would be kept down. That principle applies to health insurance for the nation as it applies to life insurance for a limited group of people.
I do not feel it is necessary to argue the principle of this matter. What we seem to have to argue for is to get action out of the present government. The only reason I can see for the government holding back is that the government might have the false notion that the people of Canada do not want national health insurance. I am convinced that they do. As the minister will recall, during the course of this session he and I were privileged, along with one or two others, to participate in what I thought was a very interesting "Citizens' Forum" discussion which was carried by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
In terms of "Citizens' Forum" discussions it was one of the most interesting in which I had ever participated. We did not do much preparation in advance. We were not too sure before we started what line each of the participants was going to take. The Minister of National Health and Welfare surprised me a bit. I found he was pretty well on my side, that the two of us were arguing for some form of nation-wide health insurance as opposed to a differing point of view which suggested that it should be done on a voluntary basis. The minister can correct me if I am wrong, but I think it is fair to say that he took the position that, some advantages though there might be in voluntary plans, they could not possibly cover the entire nation, could not possibly cover all the people of this country, and that sooner or later we had to get some form of nation-wide health insurance with government participation, including both the federal government and the provinces.
I am not going to bore the house with what the minister and I had to say on that occasion, but I was more than interested in a broadcast which was given in the "Citizens' Forum" series on Thursday, April 1, 1954, during which C.B.C. speakers summed up the reaction of the forum groups across the country to a number of "Citizens' Forum" discussions that were conducted during the course of the 1953-54 season. I found that the "Citizens' Forum" groups provided some very interesting information for the C.B.C. people when it came time to report on the discussions. For example, I find this, which was said, as I say, over the C.B.C. on April 1 of this year:
Saskatchewan is the only province where a majority of the groups feels that present services

in their community are fairly adequate. Everywhere else-even in large cities like Montreal- there would appear to be a good deal of dissatisfaction and concern. Listeners don't criticize the existing medical and hospital plans, as such. Indeed, some point out that they are rendering excellent service. But they don't believe that they provide for the people who really need protection most. The costs make them quite out of reach for poorer families-they argue-and they're uncomfortably high too for many in the middle income group- who have always had the worst of the medical deal -according to some maritime listeners.
That is just a sampling or a collection of opinions from across the country, indicating that the people who listened to our broadcast generally felt that the services we have now got are not sufficient and that the main problem is cost. Then I come to this interesting paragraph:
Under these circumstances it was interesting to see the reaction of the B.C. forums to the topic ''What Health Plan for Canadians'', and especially to the question of government participation in such a scheme. Surprisingly enough, every one of the forums-
The reference is to the British Columbia forums.
-favoured a compulsory national plan to cover every Canadian. The only disagreement was over the best method of collection of the necessary fees. While 60 per cent favoured the use of premiums, 20 per cent wanted the costs to come from general taxation. But the point that snagged all of the discussions was that though all Canadians are in need of medical care, not all are equally able to pay. Any health plan must cover this latter part of the population, but without imposing higher expenses on the rest of the people. We are all looking forward to the day when a government can solve that one.
My reason for reading these one or two excerpts from this summary that was given over the C.B.C. is that I think it gives, as nearly as one can obtain it, a report of what ordinary Canadians are thinking about this question of health insurance. I believe these excerpts which I have read represent pretty well what the average Canadian is thinking. He thinks the health services we have got are fine as far as they go. Many Canadians feel great debts of gratitude to doctors who have ministered to them and have saved their lives. Many Canadians are grateful for such hospital services as we have in this country. But Canadians generally are also very much aware of the heavy costs of medical care and how unfairly those costs impinge upon those in the lower and middle income brackets. You find, therefore, an increasing number of Canadians with the very strong feeling that the only possible solution to this matter is a nation-wide program of health insurance.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark on this question. Earlier in my remarks today I read the 83276-399
Supply-Health and Welfare amendment of my leader, moved on November 16, and I still find it difficult to know why he and his colleagues voted against these words:
We further represent that this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation.
Quite a few social security measures as well as other measures, Mr. Chairman, have got started in this country precisely on that basis, on the basis of federal legislation making possible provincial participation as and when the provinces wished to come into such a plan. It was that way we got old age pensions in the first place. Not all the provinces came into the plan at the start. I believe it was more than a decade before all the provinces were in the original old age pension plan. Without bothering to produce other instances in the interim, I point out that only a week or two ago we passed another social security measure on that same basis. I refer to the bill providing for allowances for disabled persons. It is a federal measure with provision for provincial participation, and it will come into effect only in those provinces that are prepared to join in it and to pay their share of the costs. At least in respect of that measure we have reached a point where Canadians in other provinces are not going to be told they have to wait longer because all the provinces are not ready.
Why can we not apply that same principle, that same modus operandi, to this question of health insurance? If there are, as I believe, a number of provinces whose people would like to see a health insurance program started, let us have exactly what we asked for in that subamendment, despite the fact the Liberals and Conservatives in this house voted against the proposal that there be federal legislation setting up a nation-wide health insurance program with provision for the provinces to participate in it, and to administer it, when the provinces are ready to do so.
The minister and members generally know of my own keen interest in social security matters. They know that I never miss an opportunity to advocate higher old age pensions and other forms of social security involving the placing of actual dollars in the hands of those who need them. I am not announcing anything when I indicate I shall continue to advocate increases in those other social security measures. But, Mr. Chairman, I want to say that, in my view, when we are dealing with health insurance we are
6304	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare dealing with the most important item in an over-all social security program. It is the most serious gap in our program at the moment. It is the matter about which something must be done.
I urge upon the minister, as strongly as I can, that he carry on his fight. I believe he is fighting for it inside the cabinet-goodness, that must be an awful place to fight- and I urge him to carry on the fight for this most important improvement. Surely, with all of the capacity that we have for producing wealth, with all of the capacity we have for arranging our economy so as to meet the needs of defence or some of the needs of peace as they come along, it does not make sense that we have not found a way to devote an appropriate portion of our national wealth to the provision of the best possible health care for all our people.
Let us not have any quibbling about the cost of it. As the hon. member for Mackenzie said this morning when we were talking about burnt-out pensions, if a request came along, even before the end of this session, for another $100 million or $200 million or even more for NATO, the government would consider it very seriously. I would not be surprised if they asked for it before the end of this session. Why quibble over a corresponding amount that could be devoted to such an important question as this? It is not a case of giving our people something for nothing. All the wealth of this country, all the money this government or any other government has to spend has been created by our people through their work and their toil. They deserve, because of their work and toil and because of the wealth they produce, immediate action to make sure that a proper portion of that wealth will be devoted to this most important cause, the care of our health. I insist that the time has come for action by this government on the question of a nationwide health insurance program.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
My remarks, Mr. Chairman, should not occupy the house for more than a few minutes this afternoon. After all, thus far during the session, we have had an opportunity of discussing a number of matters which would properly fall within the scope of this department. Moreover, with respect to the question of health insurance, we did have an extended debate during the month of November. However, I do intend to make a passing reference to that in a moment.
Previous speakers have indicated their belief in the importance of the Department of National Health and Welfare. We concur in those observations. We have said upon more than one occasion in this house that it is our belief that the health of the people is
CMr. Knowles.!

the nation's greatest asset. We are convinced that without good health all else would be of little avail. We are convinced also, and are not overlooking this fact in any way, that vast strides have been made in this field of health and welfare in Canada. When I was speaking in this house on November 26 last, I emphasized that belief of ours.
After all, when one stops to consider what is being done by the federal government in national health and welfare, by the provincial governments of the ten provinces, by the municipalities, by the voluntary health organizations, by the doctors, the nurses and those administering the hospitals, one cannot help realizing that the picture is a vastly improved one as compared with that of not very many years ago. And in speaking of the federal government, the provinces, and the like, I should have pointed out that it is not only a question of their working individually and independently to a certain degree, but of all of them working co-operatively to accomplish this most desirable result.
Having said that, however, I must hasten to add that there are some things which do not concern us very greatly. The hon. member for Lanark referred to the importance of research, and in doing so made mention of the infant mortality rate within this nation. I am not certain of the figures to which I shall refer. It may be that I am quite wrong, but I read recently that among the nations of the world we rank thirteenth, so far as infant mortality is concerned. In other words there are 12 nations with lower infant mortality rates than we have.
That staggers me. After all, when one stops to consider the very nature of this nation, the high standard of living we enjoy within the nation, our expanded facilities for health services, and the like, he cannot help asking himself why we should be thirteenth. I would ask the minister to deal with that matter during the consideration of these estimates. I am confident that others have been staggered by that information.
The hon. member for Lanark referred to another point to which I shall now turn. Anyone who will pick up a newspaper will observe the number of persons in middle life who, to use a common expression, just drop dead from heart condition. I wonder what research has been conducted in that field. Only a day or two ago I picked up a local newspaper and, on various pages of that newspaper, I found deaths recorded. I knew none of these people. One young man was 41 years old, another was 43 and a third was 47. Upon reading reports of these deaths

it became clear that these three at least- and there may have been others in the same issue of the newspaper-simply died suddenly as a consequence of heart disease. I would ask the minister to indicate to us just to what extent that particular aspect of our national health problem is being attacked, right at its roots.
I have certain ideas, myself. I am sure the minister had, too, when he engaged in his particular program of weight reduction. I have tried to follow the lead and with very happy results. However, I do hope the minister will comment upon that aspect of the whole problem.
I am not going to make reference to many other subjects, apart from that of health insurance, because I do know there will be opportunity to deal with most of them under the individual items. Each time I hear health insurance discussed I become just a bit more confused. I ask myself this question: Is it health insurance, or is it sickness insurance that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is actually talking about? I have been compelled to come to the conclusion that he is talking about sickness insurance, provision for people who become ill, rather than health insurance.
The most important problem facing us in Canada is not the sickness aspect, important as it may be: it is the cause of illness, the prevention of illness, which in my view is of prime concern. That is why, whenever we have talked of any health program in Canada, those of us in this group have laid emphasis upon the preventive aspect, that of teaching the people how to live so that they may not become ill. Because, after all, when people become ill the problem has been created and the damage has been done.
Let us not concentrate our attention upon sickness insurance, but rather upon a broadened health program which shall have as one of its prime purposes that of keeping people well. I agree with the hon. member for Lanark that we do not want what I believe both he and I call state medicine. I realize that state medicine will offer certain things. For example, I would not want the British program as it stands today. While there are aspects of it that are good, I see serious weaknesses in the British scheme. And certainly I think some of its weakness has resulted from the fact that the state has gone altogether too far into that field.
We realize fully that at least for people in certain parts of the country hospital costs are extremely high. One thing that bears down upon my mind when I am here in Ottawa is the knowledge that if I become ill 83276-399i
Supply-Health and Welfare I shall have to pay a very heavy cost for the privilege of occupying a bed in one of the hospitals. That is not such a heavy burden when I am at home because I can have that accommodation for a dollar a day.
I mention that for this reason. It occurs to me that costs to individuals who occupy hospital beds could be reduced by methods other than that of putting into effect an over-all sickness insurance scheme. I feel that grants payable to hospitals-grants which, after all, come out of the contributions of all the people of Canada-should be used toward reducing the cost of hospitalization to those requiring it. That scheme prevails in certain parts of Canada, without premium charges being imposed upon individuals as such. And when I talk about premium charges I would say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I am a bit confused as to whether he does actually advocate a contributory scheme or whether he advocates a scheme which would be financed out of the general revenue of Canada.
Today in connection with health insurance he quoted with approval certain statements, and throughout those statements I noticed the word "contributory" was rather heavily underlined. Yet I reminded him that last November 26, in introducing their amendment, they said, "We believe the plan should be financed out of the federal treasury"-or "out of the general revenue of Canada". I believe that was the actual expression used.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: All of which comes from the contributions of the Canadian people.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Yes, that is true; but let us not forget that there is a fundamental difference between financing out of the general revenue, the consolidated revenue fund, and imposing a premium levied upon individual Canadians, earmarking those premiums and then paying them out for services rendered. In the discussion of this whole matter let us not forget that there are certain group insurance plans in operation in Canada. All of these apply to groups, but there are certain others such as Blue Cross. If consideration is to be given to this problem, then consideration might be given to this question of subsidizing certain of the schemes in order that the cost may be brought down to where it can be handled by the rank and file of the people of our country.
This might be of interest to hon. members. I recall that at least thirty years ago in the town in which I resided a voluntary organization of citizens came into being. The doctors worked closely in connection with this voluntary organization. Each family paid $25 into the scheme and each family

Supply-Health and Welfare was entitled to all medical services, apart from the treatment of venereal disease. I think that was the only exclusion. Today, after more than thirty years, that scheme is still in operation although-and I am speaking from memory now-I believe the charge per family is now $35. It is wholly voluntary. The family comes in under the scheme of its own free will. If it does not, it pays normal prevailing charges. Naturally, they have to pay before a certain day each year. The doctors voluntarily came into the scheme; there was no pressure in any way whatsoever. In fact the doctors had a good deal to do with initiating the scheme. There is nothing to prevent the doctors from taking cases outside the scheme. It is still in operation, and I think operating satisfactorily. In fact, speaking from memory once again, I believe there are two such organizations within that community, a town of about 2,500 people. It also takes in the surrounding community. I have often wondered-

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: That is Stettler?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
No, Cardston, Alberta. There may be others in Alberta. The hon. member for Acadia says something similar is operating in Drumheller. It occurs to me that probably there is a field that the medical profession should explore. Perhaps they have already done so, but to me it offers much; it guarantees freedom to patients and to the doctor. The hon. member for Lanark, as a representative of the medical profession, indicated that he wanted those things preserved, and certainly I do, too.
Certainly I think the medical profession of this country realize that they are under pressure. I think a good many of them do realize that this pressure is bearing in from all sides, and just when the Minister of National Health and Welfare or his government may weaken, I do not know-weaken in the sense that they may be prevailed upon to go a whole lot farther than they should go into this field of national health insurance.
I say to the medical men, much is going to depend upon you. I commend the type of scheme to which I referred. There may be others which are even better, but let me repeat what I said earlier. We feel that medical and hospital costs could, generally speaking, be brought within the Canadian people's ability to pay, without the regimentation of those Canadian people, without setting up another broad comprehensive administrative organization, costly as they all prove to be sooner or later. Let me say this to the minister. I trust that he as Minister of National Health and Welfare will never be guilty of simply foisting a scheme upon this house and say, take it or leave it. I trust


that, if this health insurance study program advances to the point where the minister and the government may think "Well, now, it is time to do something", they will follow the same course of procedure that was followed in consideration of old age pensions, and that a committee of this house or a joint committee of both houses will be set up and be permitted to make a comprehensive study, and call in witnesses.
I am not too impressed by what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said about the views of these forums. I should like to know the membership of these forums. I should like to know where they are located, not only provincially, but where within the provinces. I cannot put too much value on that report until I know more about it. But I do know this. If a joint committee is set up-and I have served on a number of those joint committees-all interested national organizations are allowed to appear and make their representations on behalf of the people of this country. If that is done we shall find out pretty definitely what it is that the people of this country desire.
I know that a petition was circulated in the country not very many years ago. I saw a pile about two feet high on one of the desks of this house; but, Mr. Chairman, that did not impress me, because I for one was never told just exactly what the individual who signed was told or asked. Not only that: it is very easy for one to say, Yes, I want health insurance. But it is quite a different thing when it comes to discussing health insurance or a health program with him and finding out just what particular program he wants.
I stated last November, when we contemplated voting for the C.C.F. subamendment, that we did not want it thought for one moment that we were accepting any specific program that they or anybody else might come up with. We wanted a broadening of health services across the country. I think all hon. members desire to see something like that, but it certainly did not commit us to any specific program.
I should like to see someone in this house, who really wants health insurance, get up some time and give a fairly comprehensive outline of that which he wants us to accept, because the term "health insurance" can mean just about all things to all men, and I should like to know a little bit more about the details of any proposals.
We have said-and I shall repeat it quickly-we believe firmly in the maintenance of individual responsibility, self-help, as it were. I know that the people of this country desire to help themselves. They want to retain that. Certainly, we want to retain

the freedom of the doctors and the nurses and the hospitals, and the administrators of the hospitals in the sense that they are elected representatives of the community.
I have laid emphasis before on preventive medicine. In spite of all that has been done, we have slipped back as far as preventive medicine is concerned. I am not depreciating for one moment what the minister's department has done in this field; I am not depreciating for one moment what the provincial departments have done. But I still say that we are lagging behind as far as preventive medicine is concerned, with the result that all across the country people are talking health insurance when they mean sickness insurance. Well, let us attack this thing at its root; let us concentrate more and more on keeping people well.
I am going to say something in a moment about voluntary organizations, and it will be in connection with that. I have said that no matter what program is brought in, whatever services are extended to the people of this country, such can be financed by the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities. Decentralize administration as far as it is possible to do it. Let us have administration on the lowest possible level. Precedents have already been established in this field. Health grants are paid to the provinces for hospital construction. I believe the province matches that dollar for dollar, and the two put together will not build the hospital, and therefore the municipality-if it happens to be a municipal hospital-or whatever the local supporting body may be, will put up the remainder. That hospital is administered at a local level under the provisions of the provincial act. I have always felt and still feel that we should keep the administration there as close to the people as we possibly can if for no other reason than that when things do not go as they should the administrators will be close enough to be kicked where they will feel it most.
I said a moment ago that I trust we will not come into this parliament some session and have some scheme of health insurance suddenly slammed before us. I think the minister followed the proper course in consideration of the old age pension and, for example, in consideration of the veterans charter. This is another field in which that procedure should be followed.
From time to time in this house the minister has paid tribute to voluntary health organizations in this country, but I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that the minister's actions are certainly not a true reflection of his statement in this respect. Indeed, I do not have to go beyond the item provided in
Supply-Health and Welfare these estimates for the voluntary health organizations in this country. One would have to be blind to fail to see the important work that has been done and is still being done by these organizations in this country. But instead of the government creating the impression that they are finding less value in the work of these organizations as time goes on they should, in my opinion, convey to us their belief that these organizations can play an even more important part in the future. Some of these organizations are getting less in grants than they got years ago and some of them operate from year to year with what is nothing more than a paltry sum.
The minister must know that there are more people to be served by these organizations and he must know that their costs, including even postage, have gone up. He must know they are obliged to pay sales tax on many of the things they use to carry out these services. What the minister is indicating is that they should do as much today with their present revenues as they did years ago. That, of course, is fantastic. It seems that the minister has lost part if not all of his appreciation of our voluntary health organizations. Perhaps there is some other explanation but I for one simply cannot understand the present attitude.
The minister, with all the additional burdens which have been placed upon his shoulders, including civil defence covering an amount of $6 million in the estimates, should be tickled to death to see the voluntary organizations taking over more and more of the work in the field of health and welfare which they are perfectly competent to do. I do not think they are looking for any glory. But if there is any glory then the minister can share it.
I think I have given a fair expression to my views on this matter but when we come to deal with these items the minister should anticipate that I am going to put some rather searching questions to him. I said at the commencement of my remarks that while I may criticize I can also pay tribute. Vast strides have been made in this country in the field of health and welfare and I say that with conviction. I will give the minister all the credit in the world for the accomplishments which have been brought about. I think his heart is in the right place but we will still hope that he will not allow any group or body in this country to push him or his department into what I call state medicine.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a question or two to ask the minister. We
6308	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare have all heard about the prevalence of cancer, heart disease, infant mortality and tuberculosis, but we have heard nothing about the causes. I know it is not popular to state what the causes are but I will give my own explanation. Today we spend $868 million on liquor. I know a person can take a drink without hurting anyone. We also spend $465 million on tobacco. A person can take a smoke and not hurt anyone. But we know that many of these illnesses come from hangovers. Lots of people in Canada do not touch drink, but there are many who do and there are lots of these hangovers which hang, as I have found from experience in dealing with many of these people. I say that the $868 million spent on liquor is the cause of mental illness and t.b. and it certainly is the cause of a lot of heart-burning.
My friend the former member for St. Boniface, Dr. Howden, now Senator Howden, told me "Put this in your pipe and smoke it. There are a lot of people who will suddenly drop dead because they are heavy smokers." He said that one of the greatest causes of heart trouble was the use of tobacco. I congratulate the minister on having organized some research along these lines. We are spending $1,333 million on something which does not do anyone any good and we could have health insurance for that amount of money. But my question is, can the minister give us the outstanding causes of cancer, t.b., heart trouble, and infant mortality?

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure that if the minister could answer the questions posed by the hon. member for Fort William he would not be sitting here but in a laboratory somewhere drawing a lot of money. However, the figures the hon. member gave in regard to expenditure on liquor and tobacco perhaps add up to the principle enunciated by the hon. member for Red Deer, that this is a matter of individual choice. You can drink or smoke yourself to death if you so desire.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: It is a question of individual freedom and of course we might as well smoke here as in the hereafter.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
It is rather unfortunate that a debate such as this, which means so much to the people of Canada, should take place in the dying days of the session when so many things which are not so important to our people are dragged along from day to day resulting in a great waste of time.
At the outset I want to say that when the hon. member for Lanark was talking and I asked him to define "state medicine", I was


not being offensive. He is one member in the House of Commons whose opinion I value highly on any subject pertaining to the health and welfare department. But I have heard that term thrown around rather loosely not only in connection with health insurance but in connection with many other matters. Any time that the suggestion is made that the government should be interested in any particular matter, someone starts to say, "Oh, that is socialism". I think that propaganda about "state medicine" emanated largely from the American Medical Association, but nobody ever defines it much. It is just a catchword that has been thrown around without anyone stopping to consider exactly what it means.
To my mind the situation in Canada today with regard to the health of our people and their ability to get any kind of health services, after at least 50 years of our present medical set-up, is such that it makes necessary some form of concerted action on the part of governments to ..try to sort out some kind of mechanics whereby it will be possible to bring to the people who need it the medical science that is now available. It has certainly been proven that neither the voluntary health organization nor the free, unrestricted system that many people like to claim is best has measured up to the requirements. There is a big gap there and that gap must be filled by someone. That someone must be the organization which has the facilities, the finances and the personnel with which properly to plan that over-all scheme. For my money, the only agency in Canada that is able to fill that gap is the federal government. We do not need to quibble about that matter; that fact has been fairly well proven.
As to the matter of money, although we used to quarrel about this question I do not think we should quarrel about it any longer. Before the last war a million dollars looked like a great deal of money, and money was a mysterious, elusive thing that was hard to get. But when that war broke out we did not have any difficulty in getting money. It is too bad we could not drive that principle home to Malenkov and all others who try to make war.
I was just looking at a return that was tabled in the House of Commons for the hon. member for York South on the cost of the last two wars. We spent $22,482,036,080. That figure does not take into consideration the interest, nor does it take into consideration the loss of life: 60,000 young Canadians in the first war and 45,000 in the last. That is just the actual money involved.

Yes, dollars and cents, without counting the interest. We now find ourselves in this position, in the kind of world in which we are living. If we are forced into that kind of thing again, we will not measure in terms of dollars and cents the services this country will render in that field.
I was looking over-and this is a good witness to call-the monthly letter of the Royal Bank of Canada. They are not particularly radical; they are not socialistic. This letter was put out in January. It was their contribution to national health week. I should like hon. members to remember this when we think in terms of government, the state and the nation. In the first paragraph of that news letter they had this to say:
Conservation of life is foremost among material things in the minds of men. Benjamin Disraeli, one of history's most distinguished practitioners of political science, remarked: "the health of the people is the foundation upon which all their happiness and all their powers as a state depend."
Unless you have healthy people, you have not a healthy nation. When we are talking about this subject, let us remember that fact and put it in its proper perspective. In the final analysis, the most important subject that the House of Commons can consider-and let us divorce it from dollars and cents-is the health of the Canadian people. How good is that health?
This monthly letter of the Royal Bank gives us a few figures. I think they fairly well pinpoint the fact that the great majority of Canadians cannot afford any kind of health services. They give us some dominion bureau of statistics figures, and I am going to quote them:
Out of an estimated ii million family units, there were 621,000 which spent nothing for medical, dental, hospital or any other sort of health care during that period, while 757,000 spent less than $20. Beyond that sum the figures were:
between $20 and $49	 938,000
$50 and $99	 994,000
$100 and $199	 839,000
$200 and $499	 343,000
over $500	 63,000
I think those figures reveal the fact that almost half of that group are getting no medical care whatsoever. As to the group in which from $200 to $499 was spent, I think those figures represent the average that should be spent by every Canadian family. No family which is not spending that amount of money on checking up on the teeth and proper examination-and this is where my friend's preventive medicine comes in-is spending what is necessary. That is the amount of money necessary to be spent in any family if you are going to call a doctor
Supply-Health and Welfare in for the ordinary ills of children from a year old up to about 15 years of age, when you must get their tonsils fixed up, their eyes looked after and their teeth properly cared for. If you are getting away with $200 to $400 a year, that is about normal. You are not spending what you should spend, but that is about the average that I think should be spent. Look at the terrific number of people who are spending under that amount and who are not able to spend anything.
I want to tell my hon. friend, for whom I have a great deal of respect-and he is a good friend of mine-that the only way to have preventive medicine is to have a system whereby the average family can call in a doctor when slight signs of some disability appear. It is too late for this to be done when there is a raging fever or when some disease has become fully developed. The only way in which to get preventive medicine is to make medicine and doctors available to people for proper examinations before real trouble develops.
With respect to the ability of the provinces to handle the problem, it has been the policy for some considerable time to let them look after it. But the provinces are not able to take care of the problem, and I think that has been very clearly demonstrated in the national health grants. I have in my hand the answers to two questions asked by the hon. member for York South, which answers were given on January 25, 1954. He asked two questions which make clear the ability of the provinces to look after health services even with the grants made at the present time. These were the questions:
1.	What is the amount that was available for each province for each year since 1948 under the federal health grant program?
2.	What is the amount that was actually paid to each province for each year since 1948 under that program?
The figures are given for all the provinces but I am not going to take the time to put them on the record. Over the period from 1948 to 1953 the total amount of money advanced to the provinces under the health grants was $93,981,553. What amount of money was available? The amount available to the provinces during that period was $167,407,851. Over $167 million was available under these matching grants and the provinces only took something over $93 million. They are not able to match the grants dollar for dollar as is mandatory.

speechtext:
That is right, either the one or the other. But in my opinion these figures definitely dispel the illusion that a solution can be found under any kind of scheme other than an over-all national health plan worked out in co-operation with the provinces, with the administration left to the provinces and the financing and direction left in the hands of the federal government, because they seem to be the only agency that has the money to do the job.
Voluntary organizations were perhaps all right at their inception, but the health problem has increased to such an extent that they are no longer able to do very much about it.
I am not going to criticize any particular organization but I am going to give an example right in this city. I am going to take the case of the civil servants, most of whom live in Ottawa. They have the Blue Cross and civil service plans available to them, but after having insured themselves for hospitalization they find themselves in the position that they cannot get into a hospital. At the Civic Hospital there is a waiting list of from 1,500 to 1,700, and at the General Hospital there are another 1,500 to 1,600 applications. Bed space is not available.


These organizations are selling hospitalization insurance and they are not able to provide hospitalization. You will find many civil servants in this city who are paying for both the Blue Cross and the civil service health plans, but when there is illness in the home that requires hospitalization they are not able to get a bed in a hospital and therefore they have got to make a little hospital in a room at home. They call a doctor and they pay $3 for each visit he makes. They hire a nurse if it is necessary. They are not protected against the cost of such an illness at home even though they are paying under two hospitalization schemes.
If the patient is in a hospital the doctor's fee is paid while the patient is hospitalized, but if the organization that is selling the insurance cannot provide the hospital space they do not pay the doctor's fee for attendance on the patient in his own home. I say that these organizations are selling a commodity that they are not able to deliver. While there are many good people at the head of these organizations, and while their intentions are good, the problem of health so far as hospitalization and doctors are concerned has increased to such an extent that these organizations are not able to deliver the goods. In my judgment the only answer is an over-all health program.
With respect to the question of the name, I am not particular what you call anything if it provides the service, and I do not care much what somebody thinks about state medicine, nationalization and so on. I say that because the great majority of the people who use these terms loosely are merely repeating propaganda they have been subjected to over the years without taking very much time to think the matter through or to read authoritative works on the subject.
Let us take an example we have right in Canada. Let us take our veterans hospitals throughout the country. I am sure that no hon. member would say that these hospitals are state controlled and subject to dictatorship and regimentation. In every province of Canada the best hospitals are the veterans hospitals. No private hospital has the equipment you will find in the veterans hospitals, and in each one of these hospitals they have all the necessary services. They are built near university centres. They have the services of the university people and the best doctors in the Dominion of Canada who are found in the areas adjacent to these hospitals. That is paid for out of the consolidated revenue fund. On this question of contributory or non-contributory, I may say that is contributory. The taxpayers of Canada contribute towards it. We have a graduated

iax structure in Canada under which he who makes the most pays the most. It is as close as you can get to a taxation system for that purpose of helping to pay for these hospitals. These hospitals are working well. They are fully staffed, and their services are unlimited. Improvements are made from month to month as they come along and new equipment and new techniques are adopted.
In considering other institutions, I do not need to go outside of my own area. We have had a panel system operated on a co-operative basis for a good many years. In this instance, we are paying to keep well. We pay the doctor and the hospital approximately $130 a year between the two of them. We pay that when we are well, and when we are sick both the doctor and hospital are available to us for as long as we are sick. There is no limit to it. These institutions are certified, they are up to date and they meet the requirements. While that is so, the report on them for the past twenty years has been one increase after another in the rates. The services and equipment are deteriorating and the hospital is going further and further into debt all the time.
The hospitals in that area today are in the position where they are asking for either the provincial or federal government to help them to keep their doors open and maintain some kind of service. In the face of that, something has to be done. The only agency of which I am aware is this agency, the federal government.
Now, if anyone wants a definition of the kind of thing we have in mind by way of a national health service for this country, I may say that my conception of it is the sort of thing that has been done in our veterans hospitals. If we can do that for the veteran population, there is no reason why we cannot do it for the civilian population right across this country. I hope the time is not far distant when, instead of those inside this house or outside of it quarrelling about terms and about regimentation, we try to get our heads together and develop a system in this country whereby we can make the benefits of medical science available to all our people.
I recall that in 1944 I had the privilege of visiting France for a short time. I spent an evening at a big military hospital near Saint-Malo. There was a group of Canadian doctors there, and before we left there was one little fellow who sat down and said, "I should like to talk to you fellows before you go". He asked what progress we had made in Canada on this question of an over-all medical scheme and I said, "We are doing a lot of talking about it, but we have not done very
Supply-Health and Welfare much about the actual mechanics of it". He said, "I hope you will". "You know," he said, "before I came into the army I was practising medicine in a city in Canada and I specialized in abdominal surgery. I had a little office to myself. I was not on the hospital board, so I could not work in a hospital. I had two miracle bottles, one on this shelf and one on the other shelf, and when people came in to see me, I knew a lot of them needed surgery. I could not afford to give it to them, and they could not afford to buy it. When the war broke out my qualifications were checked, they sent for me and I went down to Ottawa. I put on a uniform and they made me a lieutenant colonel. I came over to England, went into a hospital and found myself with nurses at my disposal. I found myself with laboratories, technicians and all kinds of equipment of which I had dreamed. My wife was receiving an adequate allowance and I was receiving a salary cheque. I no longer had any economic problem, and I began to think in terms of a doctor. I was really a doctor. I had heard a lot about the question of state medicine before I came into the army, and I was scared to death of it, but I am convinced this is it; this is the kind of thing about which the people were talking. I hope when the war is over you will not scrap all this wonderful equipment we have built up, so that when I leave the army I will have to go back to those two miracle bottles". That was his conception of it, and it is true. I say that merely for the purpose of trying to get this business of terms straightened out.
I do not think there is any quarrel amongst very many of us in this house about wanting to get something done. We will not get anything done as long as we continue throwing this kind of talk across the house to the minister, who I know wants this sort of thing done as badly as any of us. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was quite right when he said the minister has to fight the treasury board on this question. I do not believe money should be considered when we are considering health. I believe that medical science in Canada is available in abundance if we would only unharness it from the economic disability under which it now exists. I believe the federal government can do the job if some of the provinces would give up this wish to preside over a little domain they have.
I rose, Mr. Chairman, with the intention of saying something else, but in listening to the discussion I was led to make these remarks. The subject I wanted to discuss is one that I know the minister would rather leave until another time. However, it is

Supply-Health and Welfare so quiet this afternoon, and everyone is in such a receptive mood, I feel it would not be a bad time to get it on the record and let other members think about it. I believe it would be very helpful to the minister. I have another thing in mind. On March 12 the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys suggested to me that I might leave a certain discussion on his estimates until the item for the coal board was under consideration. I have been waiting since March 12 for a statement of policy on that subject. While I have all the faith in the world in the honesty and integrity of the minister, I still believe this is a very good time, in this quiet atmosphere, to get this subject off my chest.
I believe it is important because, like health insurance, the matter of civil defence is a controversial subject. It is mentioned in all the newspapers, and has been debated in the British House of Commons. I have read a lot of statements about it. The statement that impressed me the most was made by Sir Winston Churchill to his own House of Commons. He warned them not to fool themselves by scrapping everything they had built up by way of civil defence. He told them not to adopt an attitude that because this atomic bomb or hydrogen bomb is a desperate weapon we do not have to do anything about it except to sit around and commit mass suicide. I disagreed with the minister-
