subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
I appreciate the minister's position. It may be that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration may have made an agreement with some hon. members who are absent from the house. Likely they will be back on Monday or Tuesday. But I have not made any commitments on that score. If the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration wants to blame me for it, I am quite prepared to take the blame. But let me say that any hon. member who wants to be away for a day or two has no right to expect me or other hon. members who are here to sit around the House of Commons waiting for him to come back to speak on any subject.
So long as my forty minutes last, I am going to discuss this subject now. I like always to bow to the will of the Chair, and I like to accommodate the minister. But this is a subject concerning which I have done considerable thinking. I might point out to the minister that I was invited to go back to my riding in connection with matters that were very important to me, but I did not go. And I did not go for the simple reason that I was expecting subjects in which I was interested to come up in the house. I had four invitations to be away-one to open a hospital, another to attend a mock parliament, which the hon. member for Nanaimo very kindly took in my place, and there were two other functions. But my place is here; and there is no other member in the House of Commons who can make an agreement for anyone else, or who can say that members who are here are not to be permitted to discuss certain subjects.

I am very sorry, Mr. Chairman, but this subject is one-the only one-in the minister's estimates that I wish to discuss. And as I am within my rights I am going to say a few words on it. And I want to say those few words for this reason, that this matter now is a controversial one-as to whether it should be under the Department of National Defence or under the Department of National Health and Welfare.
We will soon be discussing the estimates of the Minister of National Defence, and this subject will get a drilling there also.
I have thought out pretty carefully what I have to say on this subject, and because I have wanted to be careful I have made some notes. Civil defence is directed toward providing protection and security for our people in the event of war, just as the other social measures that come under the minister's department help to provide some measure of security and protection in time of peace. And on that point, as to whether it is the responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare or that of the Department of National Defence, in my judgment it belongs definitely within the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Civil defence is essentially a humanitarian activity, directed toward saving life, not taking life. For this reason it is a most appropriate responsibility for the department of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. And there is another consideration: civil defence is primarily a civilian activity. While it must be closely co-ordinated with military preparations, it is not properly a function of the armed forces.
National defence, in so far as military requirements are concerned, is a national concern and, as such, is a purely federal responsibility. But civil defence is the joint concern of federal, provincial and local authorities; and in the final analysis the main burden must rest upon the individual community, since for the most part civil defence is a matter of utilizing to the best effect a community's own services-police, fire, hospital, welfare and other facilities already in existence.
Because of the co-operative nature of civil defence, concerning as it does all three levels of government, it seems appropriate that this matter should come under a department of the federal government that, perhaps more than any other, has a record of successful co-operation with the provinces in so many areas of health and welfare activities.
Civil defence in Canada is now five years old. I do not think many Canadians would
Supply-Health and Welfare claim that we have as yet developed anywhere in this country civil defence organizations that could cope successfully with the full effects of modern warfare. But I do believe that most fair-minded persons would concede that very considerable progress has been made over the past few years. For this progress, the credit must go in large measure to the leadership provided at the federal level.
Members of the House of Commons had an opportunity to visit the new civil defence college at Arnprior a short time ago. I did not have the privilege of making that visit. On the morning I was supposed to go the committee on veterans affairs was to meet, and the chairman of the committee suggested that any members who had planned to take the trip should postpone it because important matters were being discussed by the veterans affairs committee. But my friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, made the visit and took notes of it. Upon his return he briefed me very thoroughly; and I am sure that before this debate is concluded he will have something to say as to the facilities available there.
I understand those facilities will provide for the training of approximately 2,000 persons a year. It should be acknowledged however that these 2,000, in turn, are able to train many additional thousands in their home provinces and communities. I have made some inquiries and I find that in my own province of Nova Scotia 235 persons have been trained in civil defence, many of these at federal schools and at federal expense. Perhaps this is not a large number, but it provides a useful nucleus around which to build an organization.
Another field in which leadership is coming from Ottawa is in the matter of providing certain types of equipment for training purposes which I am told now exceeds $2 million. Many of the activities now being undertaken will have peacetime value. For example, the federal authorities have agreed to pay a share of the cost of standardizing hose couplings in any province wishing to go ahead with such a plan. I am told that in some provinces there are as many as 70 or 80 different sizes, shapes and threads of fire hydrants and fire hose couplings. Obviously, without standardization one community is helpless to answer a call of a neighbour who happens to have a hose of a different size. This program would be most advantageous for normal firefighting purposes, quite apart from its civil defence application.
I note in the estimates that the grants to the provinces have been increased from

Supply-Health and Welfare $1,400,000 to $2 million. We welcome this substantial increase in federal aid available for civil defence. However, from the information I have I understand that only a small proportion of the money available was actually taken up last year. It is the same thing over again as the hospital and health grants. The provinces find themselves unable-

-to take the money that is available because they just have not got the facilities to handle it. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to tell the committee what steps he proposes to take to encourage the provinces to make fuller use of this additional money for civil defence. I want to say to the minister I am not expecting an answer now. At any time it is convenient to him, before his estimates are disposed of,
I shall be quite satisfied to get an answer to any question I am posing at this time.
Every hon. member will have been concerned over reports we have had in recent months on the destructive effects of the latest weapons devised by science. Many people are suggesting that the H-bomb and similar weapons make civil defence planning useless. The wider area of destruction that is now possible means that communities round and about the target area must be organized to come to the help of the stricken community. This means that in communities, [DOT] large and small across Canada, civil defence activities should be stepped up rather than curtailed.
The senior governments are now giving good leadership, and it is up to the authorities in individual cities, towns and villages to take whatever steps are needed to bring their local plans and programs to more adequate levels. Naturally we do not agree with everything done by the federal government in this field or in any other; but it is only fair to commend the minister on the realistic way in which this problem has been tackled over the past three years.
Now, Mr. Chairman, whether I put these remarks on the record at this time, or whether I did it next week, my reason for doing so would have been the same. I was alarmed over the attitude taken in many communities in Britain, the attitude of abandoning civil defence altogether, and that there is no defence against the hydrogen bomb. Then, there is the growing feeling in at least some sections of the press that we are wasting money on civil defence and all that kind of thing. Well, I am not one who is convinced that we are going to live in peace for the rest of our natural lives. With the arms build-up that


there is in the world today there is always the danger of someone getting trigger-happy.
As far as civil defence in Canada is concerned today, it is a matter of coming in to do rescue work. If Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto were hit, it would not be a matter of what is available in the city that counts, but what is available in the surrounding area and the availability of the equipment that will work in any section across Canada. The standardization of hose couplings is very important, and if we never have a war, the type of training that these men and women are getting today in the civil defence schools can be used in this country or in any other country for a good many years to come. Disaster can happen anywhere. The burning of the Noronic in Toronto harbour caused such casualties that it required a lot of trained assistance along those lines. Then there are mine explosions. We have had too many in Nova Scotia in the last three years, three of them to be exact, with a great loss of life. A condition of that kind requires the immediate help of those trained to assist in a disaster of that kind. Earthquakes are still not ruled out. Bad fires still break out in many communities, and the more people we could have trained in the field of civil defence work at the present time the better it would be for Canada. This should be done not only in anticipation of war; it is good training to be carried out at any time.
I am sorry I was not able to co-operate with you, Mr. Chairman, in making those remarks at this time, and I am certainly sorry I was not able to accommodate the minister. This is one subject in his estimates that I have done some thinking about, and I felt that at this time it was my right to put my thoughts on the record.

There is one other matter to which I wish to refer and to which reference has been made on a number of occasions. I would again urge upon the government and the minister the importance of giving further consideration to the matter of old age pensions.
In the Montreal Gazette of April 7, 1954, there was an article which presented very vividly the plight of many of those who are on old age pension. The article is headed, "Starved Woman's Case Shows Pensioners' Plight". I would like to read a few brief excerpts:
Out of her $40 old age pension each month, $35 was taken to pay the rent.
Supply-Health and Welfare
The remainder, five dollars, bought a month's ''supply'' of food.
Her plight, by no means an isolated case, has focused attention on the struggle of unattached pensioners to subsist on their monthly allotment.
The article then goes on to quote Mr. G. B. Clarke, general secretary of the family welfare association, as follows:
"There is no doubt about it, $40 per month is a Godsend to old people living with their families, or for those who have some additional income.
"But in this day and age, it is impossible to live on $40 alone. I would say $60 would be the very minimum for a month."
Then further down in the article we have this brief statement:
There are many old people on a bread and tea diet in this city.
And they are the most pathetic cases, living out their old age in want and poverty.
Then I would like to refer to an editorial taken from the January 20 edition of the Vancouver Province:
Now that the federal cabinet ministers and members of parliament have arranged among themselves for a handsome increase in yearly income . . . they might give some thought to the plight of people vastly poorer off than they-people who are really suffering.
I do not quote this editorial in any spirit of criticism because I am sure the house will remember that our group gave its support to the increase made at that time. However, I think I am justified in drawing the plight of these people to the attention of this house. Further on this article states:
But in the cabins and bare apartments and chill furnished rooms where some thousands of old age pensioners drag out a sorry existence, there is not even an appearance of comfort. There is just enough to get by with at the best of times, and in these freezing winter days, any penny that goes for extra heat must be deducted from the allowance for food. How could it be otherwise on a pension of $40 a month? How could it be much different even in those provinces where the pension is augmented a little?
I might point out that in British Columbia there is a $15 supplement to the pension from the province. The article continues:
If the country can afford to double the salary of a member of the Commons or the Senate, it can afford to be just, if not generous, to the people who have worn themselves out making this country and have won little or nothing for themselves in the making.
I thought it advisable to bring that to the attention of the minister to emphasize again our plea on behalf of those who are living on the old age pension. Of course there are many other cases we could draw to the attention of the government, but I feel one is sufficient, and I would just like to place myself on record this afternoon as requesting that further consideration be given to our old age pensioners. I appreciate the courtesy

Supply-Health and Welfare extended to me by hon. members in permitting me to make these remarks at this time rather than later on in the discussion.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry not to defer to the suggestion made by the minister but I promise I shall not take any longer now than I might do later on, and I will not be any duller now than I might be later on. I would like to have the same confidence as the hon. member for Cape Breton South that the quiet and peaceful atmosphere in this house means that everyone is listening. At any rate, there is a kind of calm which it is suggested to me will not be continued if we sit tonight.
I want to say a few words following what the hon. member for Red Deer said in regard to encouragement to the voluntary organizations. When we spend $816 million in the department and, I think, something in the nature of $150,000 for the voluntary organizations then there seems to me to be a terrible disparity. I want to make some suggestions to the minister along that line. The hon. member for Cape Breton South told us to forget about regimentation, get our heads together and do something. My comment on that is that I think we have got to be very clear in our own mind as to what we believe is a proper division between government activity and the activities of the voluntary organizations, and it is because I think there is a danger that the voluntary organizations-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to give an illustration of the difficulty? We are now talking about assistance to voluntary organizations. But in the estimates my hon. friend will find there are grants to the national Health League of Canada, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and other voluntary organizations, and from the limited number mentioned by my hon. friend he concludes that the grants to the voluntary organizations are very limited. But that does not give a true picture and it is only when we get into the estimates that a true picture can be given. For example, take the national health grants but under that item there are grants of $3 million to the voluntary organizations. That would not appear except when we are discussing the national health grants program. Consequently I think my hon. friend will find that he will obtain more information in the way I have suggested. I do not want to ask him to fall in with my suggestion if he feels he cannot do so, but I thought I would explain the situation.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Again I am sorry I cannot defer to the minister, but I might encourage him by saying that I shall be reasonably


brief. One of my reasons, and I think this will make him smile, is that I have not yet abandoned hope that something might be done for some of these organizations which in the midst of the universal plenty in the department are actually getting less than they got 20 or 30 years ago. It is because I wish to raise certain points which arise in my mind in regard to this that I might seem to the minister to be rather disobliging.
Now, monopoly is monopoly wherever we find it. It could be under the aegis of a socialist government, and we have an indication this afternoon that the hon. member for Cape Breton South would like it that way, or it could be under the aegis of a government that does not call itself socialist. I am sure it is not displeasing and indeed comforting to the minister to feel that over $800 million is flowing out from his department in a kind of beneficent stream which goes into hundreds of thousands of homes. I do not suppose there is any reference to authorization by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when the cheques are received, but still the people do know it, and they associate these cheques with the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Now I think this comforting thought might very easily develop into a belief that what is done by the minister in his department is really better done than it can be by anyone else, and it could easily run into the feeling that, after all, "what are these private organizations. They are very small potatoes, so why bother about them." It is because I want to suggest to the minister that the voluntary organizations are very much worth while, not only by reason of what they themselves do but by reason of what they assist him to do that I want to read onto the record one or two opinions of people whose opinions the minister will value more than he will value mine.
I think there are two main reasons for keeping these voluntary organizations alive and vigorous. The first one is to keep alive in the community those feelings which are represented by voluntary organizations, namely a sense of responsibility for other people and a quickening of the sympathy and understanding which is necessary if the community is to be the kind of vital community which it should be. In this connection I want to make reference to one or two short quotations from a book by Sidney and Beatrice Webb who, of course, approach this matter strongly from the socialist point of view but who have one or two extremely interesting things to say about the important place left for voluntary organizations. I say again, Mr. Chairman, that it is only because

of the fact that it is quite possible for this consideration to be lost sight of or to be underestimated that I take a few minutes of the time of the committee.
It is interesting to go back into the nineteenth century and to realize the two extreme and contrasting attitudes which there were in existence at that time. I am quoting now from page 222 of this book entitled "The Prevention of Destitution":
There are still many good people among us who Instinctively resent any discouragement of the personal impulse to give alms or to perform "good works" as a religious duty by which we "acquire merit" or do glory unto God, quite irrespective of the effect really produced upon the recipients and beneficiaries. To them, at least in theory, personal charity is everything. On the other hand, there are still amongst us representatives of the unspoken views of the "early Victorian" economists, who regard every kind of philanthropic action as a hideous mistake, calculated to undermine the independence and lessen the energy of the poor, and even to promote the survival of the unfit. To them, personal charity and government provision are, at least in theory, alike anathema.
We have got away beyond the idea of charity in this matter; we have got beyond it to the point of the rights of the citizen in the community, and we are now conferring benefits on the citizens of the community, not as a matter of charity but as a matter of right, which we all accept. It is because, in that situation, I think there is so much that can usefully be done by the private organizations that I wish to read another short paragraph from page 250 of the same book. The writers have just referred to the responsibility which must rest on public authorities for dealing with various types of need. Then they say:
On the other hand, though the public authority concerned must be responsible for the adequate treatment of all the cases needing attention, this does not mean that it need do, for all cases, everything that needs to be done. There is, as we shall see, an enormous part of the work which voluntary agencies can do better than the public authorities, in which they can bring to bear their specific advantages on particular cases or classes of cases, or in particular parts of the treatment of all cases. In every branch of social work, with regard to every conceivable class of case, there is the utmost need for the initiative, the inventiveness, and the practical experimenting which voluntary agencies have so much at their command.
I might read more, Mr. Chairman, but I am trying to keep this speech as short as I can.
I now wish to read an extract from an article by a man well known to the minister as well as to all who are interested in social work. I refer to Philip S. Fisher who has occupied many important positions in the field of voluntary effort. He says one or two things
Supply-Health and Welfare that I wish briefly to quote. At page 27 of Canadian Welfare of May 1, 1953, he states:
May I give you my definition of welfare? Whether it is case work or group work, whether it deals with indigency or sickness or maladjustment, the function of welfare is to make a dependent person less dependent.
Then, a little later on, at page 28 he states:
I suppose of all the differences between government and voluntary operation, the most fundamental is that a government has the power of coercion whereas a voluntary operation must rely on co-operation. Frankly, I recognize that the power of coercion must exist in certain areas, but no one will ever make me like it, or make me believe that it should be used except in situations where all other means towards uniformity of action will fail.
I value tremendously the freedom of will and freedom of action used, not in the direction of irresponsibility, but in the direction of voluntary collaboration for the benefit of the community.
And finally, from page 31:
If a government department spends $10,000, it presumably gets $10,000 worth. If it gives $10,000 to a voluntary agency, that frequently breeds an expansion of service, and of giving on the part of volunteers, with the result that twenty, thirty, forty or fifty thousand dollars may be available for welfare.
More than that, government support is a moral endorsement which can be very helpful to a volunteer operation. Here is an area where government can give leadership in advance of public opinion-at least as long as the stakes are reasonable.
As a quid pro quo, there is one service which private organizations can often perform for government departments, that is, the service of interpretation and support. Who better than the private agency can help the public agencies in interpreting their functions to the public, and in promoting their budgets? Government grants to private agencies can be good for government departments as well as for the agencies they help.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer briefly to one or two comments made regarding one of these agencies in particular, namely the Health League of Canada. Its grant has been grievously cut down. Out of a great many statements in support of the league, I wish to read briefly from three. The first is from Mr. A. R. Mosher, president of the Canadian Congress of Labour:
In this, however, as in the other activities of the league, I believe that constructive and valuable work is being done, and I have therefore no hesitation in joining in the representations which you are making to the Hon. Paul Martin, Minister of National Health and Welfare, in this connection.
Second, I wish to read a short quotation from Msgr. Ferdinand Vandry, rector of Laval University. I have the pleasure of knowing him. He is a wise and eminent citizen of our country:
(Translation):
In order to continue to fulfil its duty with efficiency, this organization needs considerable additional revenue. Accordingly I would be very happy if the Canadian government could see fit to give in accordance with the recommendations con-

Supply-Health and Welfare tained in the brief of the Canadian health league and to raise the annual grant from $10,000 to $25,000 in favour of this meritorious organization.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: Very well spoken.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Ah! thank you, sir.
(Text):
I venture to translate that quotation as follows: In order to continue to fulfil its duty with efficiency, this organization needs considerable additional revenue. Accordingly I would be very happy if the Canadian government could see fit in accordance with the recommendations contained in the brief of the Canadian health league to raise the grant in favour of this meritorious organization from $10,000 to $25,000.
Finally, I wish to read as my third quotation one from Mr. B. K. Sandwell:
I desire to extend my unqualified support to the brief of the Health League of Canada and to the league's request for the increase of its government grant to $25,000.
I am convinced that this expenditure, made through a voluntary society, will produce far better results in the education of public opinion on health subjects than any direct action by the government itself, and that these results will amply justify the grant-as indeed the results in past years have more than justified the very moderate grants which the league has received.
I just wish to end where I began. The minister is going to point out that my figure of $150,000 is not a fair comparison with $816 million. I shall of course accept the minister's correction when he gives it, but when he has made that correction I am sure that having regard to the totals involved the grants to these organizations, assuming that they are doing good work, are beggarly in the extreme. To be able to say with truth that the national health league gets half, I believe, of what it got many years ago can only be construed, so far as I can see, to mean that as we have extended public participation in welfare we have sought to dry up and lessen the work of the voluntary organizations. I hope that is not so.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
I feel that all members
who are interested in health would find it very helpful if officials from the department could be brought to one of the committee

Supply-Health and Welfare rooms here where we would have several hours in which to hear about the important work the minister is doing in the field of health.
We have had some discussion about health insurance studies. I appreciate the fact the minister cannot go much faster than public opinion will permit, but I think he can go faster than he is going. I realize that there is a good deal of opposition, particularly amongst the medical fraternity in Canada, regarding any form of socialized health service. We faced this problem ten years ago in Saskatchewan, but we have made a good deal of progress. However we have not been able to introduce a complete scheme of socialized health services because we believe in democracy and we cannot carry out that sort of program without the cooperation of the doctors.
I should like to tell the house about some of the very important fields in which we have introduced socialized health services.
I refer to cancer, t.b. and mental diseases. Saskatchewan is not the only province that has introduced socialized ideas in connection with t.b. The C.C.F. government cannot claim the credit for that. When the first sanatorium was built in Saskatchewan many years ago-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext: By Dr. Ferguson, one of the great men of Canada.

subtopic: MR. NESBITT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR WELLINGTON SOUTH
speechtext:
Yes; I appreciate that
voluntary comment from the minister. He had some new ideas regarding the treatment of t.b. He thought that the cost factor should be reduced to the minimum. When the first sanatorium was built we had a marked drop in the death rate from t.b. When the cost was reduced from $2.50 to $1 per day, there was a further drop in the death rate. Then when free treatment was introduced we had a further drop. For years Saskatchewan has had one of the lowest death rates from t.b. anywhere in the world.
I should like to submit to my medical friends that today the doctors and nurses in our sanatoria in Saskatchewan are held in very high regard by the citizens of Saskatchewan and elsewhere. I believe that, on balance, they probably have as high a standing as any doctors in the country. The same thing applies to cancer.
I am sure that many of the members will recall the former hon. member for Melfort, Mr. Percy Wright, who was here for many years. I am sure he would not mind my saying that he recently underwent a serious operation for cancer. Mr. Wright has been in the fortunate position during his lifetime


of being able to have the best medical service available anywhere in the country. Some eight or nine years ago he was advised to go to the best surgeon in Canada, the late Dr. Roscoe Graham in Toronto. He went there and underwent a successful operation. But when an operation for cancer was necessary he wanted to know whether Rochester, Toronto, Montreal or Saskatoon would be the best centre to which to go. He went to some of the best authorities in Saskatchewan, who said that making a decision as to where he should go is rather important and one should make the final decision oneself. Some of his medical friends, who were not personally interested in the case said, "If we were in your position we would stay right here in Saskatoon because we believe the people here who have been specializing in cancer have had advantages that are not found elsewhere." Mr. Wright accepted that advice, the operation was performed in Saskatoon and I am happy to say he has been enjoying very good health.
Socialized services in Saskatchewan in the field of cancer have provided for our people services which we believe cannot be surpassed anywhere in Canada. The same thing is true of mental illness, which is a very costly type of illness. In many places in Canada people who have the misfortune to become mentally ill find that all their earthly possessions are used up before they are able to earn again. In Saskatchewan those who have the misfortune to require treatment for mental illness find that the entire cost is carried by all the citizens of the province.
There is one further service I should mention, and that is the air ambulance. Again we are proud of the fact that we are the only people on this continent who have the good fortune to have a publicly-owned and operated air ambulance service available for anyone in the province if a doctor or nurse or justice of the peace or any responsible citizen expresses the opinion the air ambulance service is necessary. There is a $25 fee charged for the ambulance, with a trained nurse to go with it. It is available to go anywhere in the province to move a patient to the hospital. If the patient cannot pay the $25, the air ambulance makes the trip in any event.
I suggest that having experimented in these several fields we have come to the conclusion that the time has arrived when we should make some further progress. I might mention that I live in a municipality which has had socialized medical services for quite some time. This was a depression development when the municipality found itself in a position where it was liable for indigent

cases. The doctors were being paid $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 a year for looking after these indigent patients, upon a fee for service basis. Some of the members of the council thought if they were going to have to pay out that amount of money they should make a bargain with the doctors to pay whatever would be necessary so that everyone in the municipality would be able to have medical treatment. Again the present C.C.F. government cannot take credit for the development.
At one time about one-third of the rural municipalities in the province had municipal doctor schemes. In our municipality we have two doctors on salary. I appreciate the arguments advanced that the individual must be permitted to select the doctor. We are in the position where we can select either of two doctors, and we realize that if it were not for the municipal scheme these young doctors would probably be in Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver, where they know larger incomes are available. The young doctors out of college have been able to go to these municipal appointments. They have been able to have plenty of work from the time they come into the office. I want to tell the house that there have been very few criticisms about the quality of the service.
I have the highest regard for my neighbour, the hon. member for Lanark, who has given me some valuable training in the field of medicine since I first knew him, and who has never charged me for that medical advice. However I did not ask for any personal advice. I am sure that the people in his community have a very high regard for him. If I were to take sick tonight, and if I could get to my own doctors in Preeceville, I would rather call them than any doctor in Ottawa. Mr. Chairman, I think this is the time, before six o'clock, to put this statement on the record, so that it will be there. This is the statement of the Prime Minister on July 9 last when, speaking for this party, he said;
The Liberal party is committed to support a policy of contributory health insurance to be administered by the provinces. But, under our federal system, to get health insurance started the people and the governments of the various provinces have to take the initiative in working out plans adapted to local conditions.
We are ready to assist in a sensible and practical nation wide scheme, but that depends on satisfactory agreements with the provincial governments.
I am more convinced than ever that this is a field which should, as far as practicable, be left to provincial administration. Conditions differ vastly from one province to another, and services which are suitable for one region are quite unsuitable to another. We now have had a great deal of experience with health schemes of all kinds in this country, including full-fledged hospital insurance in two of our provinces.

Federal contributions should be regarded as a supplement and an evener-out, when most of the provinces are prepared to undertake satisfactory schemes.

Mr. Chairman, this vote has to do with the federal health grant to hospitals and at the present time the grant set by the federal authority is $1,000 per bed for active treatment, and $1,500 per bed for chronic, convalescent, mental and tuberculosis beds. That figure was arrived at when the former prime minister, the late William Lyon Mackenzie King, was in office, and he indicated that it was to be an assistance grant. At that time there was a shortage of something like 60,000 beds in this country, and I think he quoted that figure at that time.
Now before I go any further I would like to commend the people in the various communities throughout the dominion for the work they are doing in attempting to build hospitals. They are carrying out an extremely difficult task, particularly when people are being asked to contribute to every form of society under the sun. I see the minister nodding his head and I think that indicates he is aware of the difficulty.
Since the act came into effect 100 beds have been provided in the mental hospital in my own riding, as well as 169 at the Royal Columbian hospital, 48, I believe, at the Langley hospital, and there have been additions at the White Rock hospital though I am not aware of the exact number. That would indicate that the population is growing
Supply-Health and Welfare in my riding and of course hand in hand with that must go a greater need so far as hospitalization is concerned. But it is very far from true that the supply is keeping pace with the demand.
In the case of British Columbia and particularly the lower mainland the population has practically doubled within the past 20 years but certainly the number of beds for hospital purposes has not increased proportionately. Earlier in the year, speaking on the budget debate, I raised the question of the old age pensioners, and I indicated that we had to face hospitalization problems because about 6-84 per cent of the population of the riding were elderly people in receipt of old age pensions. The comparative figure in the province of Alberta is 4 per cent, Saskatchewan 4-5 per cent and Ontario, with all its wealth, has a figure of 5-3 per cent. What I am indicating is that people of that age, as everyone is aware, are more in need of hospital assistance than anyone else and we have a greater problem proportionately speaking than any other area in the Dominion of Canada.
We therefore require more assistance. In fact, the North Surrey people have been trying to build a hospital for a matter of 10 years now and each time they reach the point where they think they will be able to complete the hospital the costs go up and the actual need increases because there are many more hundreds of people in the community. Actually they have reached the stage where they have found it absolutely impossible to go ahead with the building of the hospital. This thing has been snowballing and is continuing to do so. It may be said that this is true of only one locality but I do not think that is correct.
The price of a hospital bed unit some years ago was $3,000, and in 1948 that cost had risen to $5,000 or $6,000. I understand the price today is $11,000 and the people I have mentioned are no nearer their goal today than they were 10 years ago. They are perhaps worse off because the area now requires a very much larger hospital.
The people in that area have been asked to vote money for a municipal hospital but even if they do so it will by no means be large enough to meet our needs. The White Rock hospital board has indicated that they realize that their hospital is too small already, and added to that the Langley and New Westminster hospitals are trying to raise funds in order to increase their size.
In view of the fact that a large number of people come to our province from other provinces to spend the latter part of their days

Supply-Health and Welfare ' in that region, these people feel that they should receive some further consideration, and they feel that the hospitalization vote is much too low. 1 believe there is some merit in their argument, particularly when we consider that every person in the dominion is paying only one cent towards the federal grant. They feel it should be something like two and a half cents per person. If that were done they would then become eligible for the $2,500 grant per bed. The present act says: "The hospital construction grant is to be distributed on the basis of $1,000 per bed for active treatment beds or bed equivalents in the case of health facilities, $1,500 per bed for chronic, convalescent, mental and tuberculosis beds, and $500 per bed for living quarters for nurses. The provinces are to match or exceed the federal contribution which shall in no case exceed one-third of the actual total cost."
Instead of the federal government paying one-third of the actual cost with the present cost at $11,000 per treatment bed, it means that the federal authorities are paying $1,000, which is one-eleventh, the provincial government is paying one-third, and the bulk of the cost of looking after our senior citizens is left to our municipalities. I have called attention to the fact that these elderly people are adding to the burden on the community, but we must shoulder that responsibility. In doing so, however, we require to build new hospitals and in order to do that we must have more assistance. I am sure the minister is well aware of that and while people may say that there are many people who require help I think some regions are more in need and deserving than others. I would like the minister to reply to my suggestion that we should receive at least $2,500 per bed.

My reason for rising on this particular item is to inquire whether the department could not treat the Montreal neurological institute on a more generous basis. The minister was in Montreal, as I was, on November 20. He was able to get into television there, while I had the pleasure of a seat in the gallery. I am sure he was impressed with the very able remarks by Dr. Alan Gregg who was the guest speaker on behalf of the Rockefeller foundation. Dr. Gregg said:
In but very few if any of the enterprises to which the Rockefeller foundation has been privileged to contribute in the last twenty years have the results equalled those you have created here


in this neurological institute. If I were asked to name a single grant that the medical sciences division of the foundation has made since 1931 that I consider ideal in purpose, in performance, in local response and in national and international influence, and in the character of our relationships maintained from the very beginning, I would say without a moment's hesitation the grant to the neurological institute of McGill University. But that is only one way and perhaps a trivial one of expressing the admiration and the satisfaction the Rockefeller foundation has for what you have created here. More rare still is the compliment I would offer you, not without some fear that it will fail its target, in saying that in this neurological institute, the staff, the chief and the trustees are so beautifully fused into one shining amalgam that if I were to name one to thank I would be naming you all who have worked with him, for him and through him, and if I were to name all of you it would come to the same thing-for you are all the neurological institute of McGill University, each to the other, responsible, essential and inseparable.
I am sure everyone in Canada would echo Dr. Gregg's appropriate remarks about Dr. Penfield and the institute. But I was quite disturbed when Dr. Penfield gave a review of some of their work during the year. The minister will recall that Dr. Penfield said:
It was back in 1950 at a crucial interview that the turn came in the tide of the economic affairs of this institute. Conditions had been going from bad to worse and it appeared that the doors of the hospital portion might have to be closed. We must, it seemed, get support for clinical deficits and we must rebuild and expand. There was no other way.
Dr. Penfield outlined his visit to Mr. Duplessis together with that very good friend of the institute, Mr. McConnell, and the provincial government undertook to provide $90,000 annually on condition that the friends of the institute would also do something. But it amazed me to think that as recently as 1950 Dr. Penfield, with his international reputation, had been placed in the position of having to go with cap in hand to try to get additional revenue so that their work might be carried on. In the very interesting report he gave of the work they have been doing it was made clear to me that this is one place in Canada where generous federal grants should be made.
I understand that Dr. Penfield has given up some of his activities now in the hope that he can find additional revenues so that their research work can continue. It would seem to me that with the very large amounts of money available for all sorts of things in Canada the minister should be able to give some undertaking so that this institute, which has done such outstanding work, could carry on indefinitely without these worries about balancing budgets.
On the day of the opening along with the minister and others I visited the new wing and I found there were patients there from

every province in Canada and from a number of other countries. I wonder whether the minister could not indicate whether or not this would not be an appropriate field for the federal government to make a grant on an annual basis so that the work that is being done by Dr. Penfield and his associates may continue unhampered by lack of financial resources.

This government is proud of what it has done for the neurological institute, and Dr. Penfield would be the first to say that that is the case. I should like to venture just a comment on this item. As I said on the opening item, I was very pleased to read about the development which had taken place in the industry, with particular reference to this innovation of what I think is called fish sticks or the new method of selling fillets of cod and other groundfish. According to the minister this type had attracted a tremendous amount of attention in the United States. As a matter of fact I have heard from him, and from others, that the demand was so great that the United States buyers were worried about being able to buy larger quantities of this fish rather than being worried about sales.
Having read of that, and heard that, there was a feeling that some of the problems of the fishing industry might be solved, so I was rather shocked to read in the press that apparently representations had been made to the President of the United States by the tariff commission that duties should perhaps be increased on the importation of Canadian fish. I could not reconcile the very glowing picture painted by the minister the other night with this account which I read afterwards in the press. I presume one explanation might be that the recommendations of the tariff commission had taken place before the importation of these fillets had increased to the tremendous extent it did. Either the United States is not as dependent on this as we were led to believe or else the tariff commission has made a serious mistake in making recommendations to the President or else the newspapers are reporting wrongly.

Since this is a matter that involves another country as well as our own, perhaps I should answer. I may say that as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said the tariff commission of the United States is reported to have made a recommendation to the President. As the Prime Minister informed the house on two different occasions, the Canadian government has made very strong representations on this subject. There are some encouraging features about the situation.
No action has been taken by the U.S. administration, though a report appeared in the press that recommendations had been made. In the second place, I was informed by the Minister of Fisheries himself after he returned from Cleveland, where he was the guest of a meeting of the fish trade association, that although a year ago the trade association had supported the application to the tariff commission for a restriction on the importation of these fresh frozen fillets, this year they had refrained from doing so. I understand there is divided opinion in the United States industry. Some of those who do the actual fishing, I understand, are still in favour of protection, but there are a great many United States processing firms who now get a large portion of their fish from Nova Scotia and Newfoundland in block form. Their business would be seriously interfered with if these supplies were cut off. I think we have reason for modest hope that the views we have put forward, and the views that many people in the industry in the United States have put forward, will prevail in this matter.
I certainly hope so because it would be quite disastrous, were the contrary the case, to the riding that I happen to represent, and to the whole Atlantic area. I may say, sir, that what the hon. member has said is quite correct. The demand for these fish sticks is growing more rapidly, I am told, than the demand for any other food product on this continent at the present time. I can assure any hon. member in the committee, on either side of the house, that having eaten almost a pound of them myself for dinner tonight-
At one time?
Yes, at one time-that they are simply delicious. They taste like fish that has just come out of the water. I strongly recommend these fish sticks to every member of the committee.

I am sure the people of Canada should see the radiant smile on the face of the minister. Were they to do so

they would realize what a wonderful advertisement it is for these fish. I quite agree with him that they are good.
I have one other question. Without going into too much detail in a field into which I do not wish to trespass, can he indicate, either as a result of the experience of similar recommendations in the past, or as a result of inquiries the government has recently made, when one might expect some answer would be given with respect to recommendations made by the American tariff commission to the President of the United States.

We hope no action will be taken. I think there is one very reassuring thing. I had the record examined recently and I find that the present administration in the United States has not yet accepted a single recommendation that involved action under the escape clause in GATT. I am sure everyone in the committee hopes that record will continue.
