Before I proceed to my remarks on this subject I wish to say that I was greatly interested in the discussion which took place tonight when the Leader of the Opposition mentioned the fact that we were discussing a matter which was of great importance to the Canadian people. It is always good to realize that the fishing industry is recognized as a major rather than a minor industry in this country. I am always more than pleased to hear remarks of that kind.
For a few moments this evening I should like to bring to the attention of the department a change which I believe should be made in the lobster regulations, and one which I feel is long overdue. I refer to spawn or berried lobsters which become berried after they are impounded in licensed pounds which are licensed by this department.
Realizing that there might be some opposition to this change I should like to give the committee some information in connection with this industry. Lobster pounds are a great asset to the lobster industry. During the fishing season the operators purchase lobsters to be impounded, or stored, and sold after the season closes. This has a most stabilizing effect. Without these pounds, or storage facilities, of necessity all lobsters would be offered on the open market at whatever price might be offered by dealers in all parts of the United States, particularly, because over 90 per cent of the lobsters we produce are sold in the United States.

Supply-Fisheries
One can imagine what would happen in western Canada if storage were not provided for wheat and other farm commodities. The same condition would prevail in the lobster industry without lobster pounds, or the facilities for holding them over different periods of time. Again I wish to make a few comparisons to emphasize the importance of this industry.
The impounding of lobsters by pound operators is a great gamble. You are dealing with live lobsters, a most perishable commodity, unlike farm commodities. Hundreds of thousands of dollars are invested by private enterprisers-not by the government-without any government guarantee as to price, or financial support, or anything else. Should some sort of malady strike the lobster industry, as has happened within the last few years, these operators would be obliged to take the full loss which, as I have said, would amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars.
A few years ago thousands of lobsters died in the pounds of Charlotte county, and in the state of Maine. We have yet to understand why it happened; but it did happen. The operators at that time lost hundreds of thousands of dollars, but the total loss was absorbed by the pound operators. They did not ask for government assistance. No appeal was made to the government in any case for assistance of any kind. They took their loss and stood on their own feet.
When the foot-and-mouth disease appeared in western Canada-and I suggest this is a very fair comparison-a much different view was taken. I am not saying this in any critical sense. Each and every one of us stood in our places in the House of Commons and did everything that was possible to help in that situation. I would do it again if necessary. But I just wish to make this comparison to show that these men today, the private enterprisers in this business, act in a different fashion. It is true that they are trying to make a dollar for themselves, but at the same time they are giving financial assistance to the lobster fishermen of the maritime provinces and they are receiving very little by way of assistance.
Every farmer in western Canada was fully paid for his losses when we had the foot-and-mouth disease in this country; and for that I congratulate the government upon its speedy action. Then when disaster struck the hog raisers in Ontario a year ago, again the federal government came to their assistance and the losses were sustained by the taxpayers of Canada. Again I wish to congratulate the government on the action taken in that connection.

When there is an overproduction of butter in Canada, the government purchases the surplus and furnishes cold storage. At the present time I believe there is about 30 million pounds in this position, with a guaranteed price to the producer on that butter held in storage. Again I congratulate the government on their efforts to stabilize the situation. I could also mention the $20 million which we voted just two years ago when the wheat was under the snow in western Canada. I stood in my place here and voted for that assistance to the farmers. When it came time to seed the next spring it was discovered that less than $1 million was used. Assistance of this kind has never been provided to any branch of the fishing industry.
In this industry it is a case of supply and demand, and those individuals who are making every effort to stabilize this industry receive very little encouragement. During the spring lobster season, which is in operation right now, hundreds of thousands of lobsters go into the pound for storage, to spread the supply over the twelve-month period, rather than putting them all on the market at one time, which would have a very ill effect in so far as price to fishermen is concerned. The fisheries inspector or inspectors supervise the purchase of these lobsters to be sure that each and every one is of a legal size. They are present when the lobsters are placed in the pounds. No berried or spawn lobsters may be purchased or stored in lobster pounds at any time. Every effort is made by the pound operators to comply with this regulation, and at great additional expense to themselves all the males and females are separated and placed in different compartments of the pound. It means an enormous amount of work and a lot of expense.
The approximate date that spawn or berries would appear on female lobsters is known to these owners. If they sell every female before that date and kill them before the berries appear, they have the full support of the federal government; but if some are left until after the spawn appears, any junior officer of the department has full authority to liberate every spawn lobster that may be found in the pounds, without paying the owners one single penny. We must remember, however, that these lobsters were legal lobsters when purchased. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were involved in the purchase of female lobsters during the open season, a legal procedure in every way. They were carefully inspected and passed as legal lobsters by authorized officials of the fisheries department.

In my opinion, once legal lobsters are purchased and placed in pounds they are the property of the owner. No one should have the authority to liberate a single lobster without paying the full price. The department may argue that this would encourage illegal fishing of female lobsters. I have heard that argument used. Illegal fishermen who fish for lobsters do not fish for female lobsters only, and if they catch a berried lobster the berries will be removed before it is sold. This is a very simple operation. But no fisherman is going to bring a berried or spawn lobster to a dealer and sell it. They will be removed before he brings it in. Any illegal lobsters caught in the area in which I am interested are sold on the other side of the border in the state of Maine. There, there is no restriction in so far as the lobster season is concerned. They fish twelve months of the year. It is very simple for fishermen to take their catch over the border at any season, and dispose of it at prices which would be comparable to the prices they would receive in Canada.
The department might also suggest that the change I have suggested would give pound operators advantages which are denied individual fishermen. Again I would say that you were giving the pound operator nothing. It is a matter of justice, and you are giving him the privilege of protecting his investment of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
As I stated just a few moments ago, lobsters are a most perishable article, particularly in cold weather. In the wintertime the lobster is a most delicate thing to handle. The loss sometimes is tremendous. These operators are using their own money. They are building pounds which are of great benefit to every lobster fisherman in the maritime provinces. They purchase lobsters, which are not berried at the time they are purchased. They are placed in pounds. They have paid for them with their own cash. They are impounded legally because they are inspected when they are put in there. But if berries appear on thse lobsters when they are in these pounds fo rthree months, any officials of the fisheries department can go to the pounds and liberate 10,000, 20,000 or 50,000 without paying the owner and the operator one single dollar.
I hope the department will see fit to make a change in this regulation. As I stated at the outset, it is long overdue. These men are free enterprisers. They have done a lot for the lobster industry. They have done a lot for the fishermen of the maritime provinces. I believe they must have some little consideration.
Supply-Fisheries
The regulation that we have on the statute books today could be changed very simply. All that it needs to improve the situation is to put at the end of the sentence: "except in licensed pounds". These pounds are licensed by the federal government. The licence fee is paid by the operator. I am not one of the legal profession, but I do believe that if an officer went into a legal pound today and found berried lobsters it would be hard to find a jury in the maritime provinces who would condemn the pound operator. He bought them legally; he impounded them legally and they are his own property. I believe it is time that some consideration was given to these men who are, as I say, free enterprisers, doing so much to build up this industry, and some little encouragement should be given to them.
Before I resume my seat I want to emphasize this once more. We will find some fishermen who will be opposed to this suggestion. I have fished lobsters myself. I have some idea about the industry. I have spent many hours around lobster pounds, putting lobsters in and taking them out. I have seen the loss involved in the handling of lobsters, and I realize the great risk that is taken by these men, these free enterprisers. A regulation that gives a government department authority to seize and release anything that belongs to these men, that they bought and impounded legally, is something that should be adjusted, and adjusted without any great delay.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The matter brought up by the hon. member for Charlotte is one that received the attention of the department about two years ago. At that time the department convened a meeting of all interested parties, but no unanimity could be arrived at. I might say that it is a matter of considerable controversy. The department is prepared at the present time to convene another meeting as soon as possible to see if the viewpoint of the persons opposed to the change in the regulations has changed and, if so, then a satisfactory change in the regulation may be arrived at.

I have a matter that I would like to bring up. It concerns the salmon weirs in Saint John harbour. I think I can relate it to fish economics and to this item. I mentioned it when the estimates of the Department of Transport were before the committee, but I do feel that some action should be taken. Perhaps it would be up to the Department of Fisheries to press for some remedy. It concerns the weirs on the

Supply-Fisheries
west side of Saint John harbour. I understand that they are auctioned off in three-year lots to fishermen by the national harbours board. They set an arbitrary reserve price at this auction. Perhaps they do not have the knowledge that the Department of Fisheries would have as regards the economics of the fishing and as regards conservation, and consequently when the price is not met they simply say: let the weir go, and we will not bother to use it for another three years. Three or four fishermen have brought this to my attention. They feel that a study should be made by the Department of Fisheries of the reserve prices that seem to be set arbitrarily. In some cases they feel that they are much too high. If they could be brought down to lower figures then the weirs could be worked. Some are not as profitable as they used to be in the past but the fishermen feel quite strongly about it because there is some revenue there for them and they do not like to see the weirs lying unused simply because the department really has not the full knowledge of the salmon in Saint John harbour. I wonder if the parliamentary assistant would like to comment on this and say whether he will look into the matter and take some action because if it is left up to the national harbours board I feel the situation will go on indefinitely and these weirs will be of no value in another five years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I can well understand the concern of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert in connection with these fishing weirs. As he said himself in his remarks, they are on the property of the harbours board but I can assure him the Department of Fisheries will be only too pleased to look into the matter and discuss it in all its aspects with the Minister of Transport.

Item agreed to.
132.	Administrative expenses of the Newfoundland fisheries board, $25,450.

I am wondering about the increase in regard to the Newfoundland fisheries board, perhaps merely out of curiosity. But I understand that with the reorganization of NAFEL and the new plans to hand all the marketing over to the fisheries board and hence the Department of Trade and Commerce there will be some changes in the Newfoundland fisheries board. In that event surely the board's duties would be cut down and the administrative cost would be less.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
These estimates were prepared last October before the change mentioned by the hon. member for Saint
[Mr. Bell. 3
John-Albert took place and any economies made by the changeover will be reflected in next year's estimates.

Could the parliamentary assistant tell us what the fisheries board will be doing now? To what extent are their duties and expenditures to be cut down? I understood when the announcement was made that the NAFEL organization was being completely changed. I realize this is not a government body but this is quite important and I would like to know what is being left of the entire organization.

Perhaps I should say a word about this, Mr. Chairman. The functions of the Newfoundland fisheries board with respect to marketing were transferred from the board to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but it also had other functions. The Fisheries Act has never been proclaimed in Newfoundland and the law of Newfoundland with respect to fisheries is still the old law that existed before confederation. The fisheries are administered through the Newfoundland fisheries board which is an agency of the Department of Fisheries of Canada and it has all the functions of the fisheries department to perform in so far as Newfoundland is concerned, or at least a substantial part of these functions. There may have been a few things not done before confederation that are not done through this agency but most of them are, and the only way in which the board's duties have been lightened is by transfer to trade and commerce of the supervision over NAFEL which, of course, is a private agency, as the hon. gentleman knows.

Item agreed to.
133.	Industrial development service, $1,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, as a matter of curiosity I notice that although on the face of it there appears to be a considerable decrease in this item over last year's estimate, I see on looking at the details that although there was $1,250,000 appropriated last year the total expenditure was only $350,000. Despite that the appropriation this year is $1,000,000. I wonder if the parliamentary assistant would care to explain.

I did not really intend to usurp the function of the parliamentary assistant but as the questions seem to be mainly about Newfoundland, a subject in which I have a lot of interest, I cannot resist the temptation to answer. The fact of the matter is that it was rather expected that certain developments with respect to the fisheries could be carried on a little more

rapidly than in fact proved to be possible last year. As the hon. lady no doubt knows, there was a joint committee set up by the federal government and provincial government under the chairmanship of the chief justice of Newfoundland and they made a report some time during May last year. This vote is not entirely for Newfoundland. There are certain other developments elsewhere, although the major portion of it is used in Newfoundland. The purpose there is to get on with development work in co-operation with the province, but as quite often happens in developments of this kind the planning takes a good deal longer than people expect.
Mrs, Fairclough: It seems to me that the minister has succeeded in spreading a nice thick blanket over this item because the amount for this year is still three times the expenditure which they were able to use last year. Just what type of development is anticipated that would run into $1,000,000?

As I indicated a moment ago, it is not all for Newfoundland. There are some developments in other provinces. But there is one development in particular which is perhaps of more interest to me than most of the others. It is proposed to establish an experimental dryer at a place called Valleyfield or Badger's Quay. I am not well enough acquainted with the geography of the settlement to know where one ends and the other begins, but the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, who is a constituent of mine, no doubt knows the area even better than I do. I have seen it from a ship, from the air, and from the ground and it is a very promising area for fishery development. This experimental dryer which is to be established there is going to mean perhaps as much to the salt fishery as the experimental farm means to agriculture, and it is intended to experiment not merely with drying fish but also with packaging and with new methods of preparing the product to see if a higher class of product can be produced which will appeal to a better market than has been the case for salt fish in the past.
From my rather scanty knowledge of the fishing business it seems to me that this is an industrial project. Or is it a basic government research project intended to aid the industry generally?

I am very pleased the hon. member has raised that point because there has been a great deal of misunderstanding about this very point in Newfoundland and elsewhere. The federal government does
Supply-Fisheries
not participate in the financing of commercial plants and the object of this vote is not to set up a government owned industry. It is to assist the fishing industry to develop a new type of plant for the processing of salt fish and to assist in the expansion of the fresh fish industry, and an experiment designed to assist the industry in getting into new and more profitable markets. Unfortunately, because of exchange and other difficulties, the markets for salt fish have been very unsatisfactory for the last five or six years, though there are distinct improvements this year as a result of the agreements with Spain and Portugal and as a result of the improved exchange situation in Brazil, and also as a result of the arrangement my colleague the Minister of Public Works recently concluded with Italy. However, it is felt that there is still plenty of room for improvement in the industry both in producing a good product and in finding good markets and getting what I think is called in the trade "market acceptability". I do not care much for such phrases. It is for the purpose of assisting the industry to improve its methods that this vote is used.

Either I did not make myself clear or the minister did not quite understand me. I did not for a moment mean to infer that this amount was going to put the government into the processing business or anything like that. What I intended to intimate was that this type of work, if I understand accurately the type that the minister has described, is the type of research that is usually done by the industrial firms themselves. I wonder whether this is a departure on the part of the government. If so, will the knowledge so gained be available to all of the fish packing industries in Canada, whether they are on the west coast or the east coast, or is this something that is primarily for the benefit of Newfoundland?
No. I will not say it is not primarily for the benefit of Newfoundland.
Be careful.

It is not solely for the benefit of Newfoundland. In so far as it is related to the salt codfish industry

and it is primarily related to that industry-I do not think it would be of much benefit to the west coast. But anything that is done by the federal government is done for the whole of the industry. In fact, when I was in Newfoundland last August, after the election-because unlike the hon. member for Hamilton West, I had to do my campaigning after the election instead of before it-I spent a week end at Clarenville. There were half a dozen of the leading fish processors of Newfoundland there at Clarenville the

Supply-Fisheries
first evening I was there. They spent the night there and went on the next day to Bonavista where the government has been experimenting with mechanical drying of codfish and has had some quite marked technical success. We are now trying to see whether we can get costs down so that it will be a commercial success as well.
Practically everyone interested in the processing of salt fish in Newfoundland was going down to spend the week end to examine this whole process. I was still at the same hotel when they came back at the end of the week end and I heard what they had to say about it. They went there sceptical. They came back much less sceptical. It is a new process. If it is really successful it is going to be of great help to the industry.
But it is like something else that I was fairly familiar with a long time before I became very familiar with Newfoundland. I lived in Winnipeg when the rust research laboratory was first established on the university grounds there. For a long time a great deal of money was spent without any assurance that it was going to be the immense boom that rust-resistant wheat has proved to be to the wheat industry. It is the same kind of thing that is designed for the salt fish industry.

I should like to say a word on this matter. Listening to the discussion and the explanation of the acting minister made me think back to this industry in my own county. For many years the fishermen who are interested in the dried fish industry were obliged to dry all their fish with the sun. They had nothing else to depend on but sunshine by means of which to dry the fish. Along those coastlines we have a great deal of damp weather. We came to the place where the markets were demanding a drier fish than we could produce. The moisture content of the fish which we were trying to cure in the Atlantic provinces did not meet the standards in the West Indies and other countries to which we were shipping dried fish. It became necessary for those who could afford it to instal dryers which are most expensive. I know of men on the three islands in my constituency who are in that business and who were obliged to take what we call the green fish to Saint John or to some other part of the province or of the country in order to have them dried, because they could not afford to put in the equipment which would do it properly.
This matter which is now being discussed is along that same line. In Newfoundland there is a great deal of dampness. The fish they are producing must be dried to a much greater extent than they were 10 years ago
[Mr. Piekersgill.I
or 20 years ago. We do not get sufficient sunshine to cure them. The only alternative is to instal dryers, and they are most expensive. This experimenting which they are doing in my own area-I cannot speak for Newfoundland-has been most helpful to the industry. Today we have perhaps 12 installations of dryers where 10 years ago we had none. As the fishermen are able, they will provide these additional dryers which are most necessary if you are going to stay in the dried fish industry.
I hope that the department will continue on with these experiments in that line. In my opinion items in connection with the biological board and items like the one we are now discussing come exactly in the same category as do our experimental farms in agriculture. I believe these men should be encouraged. If we are going to build up this industry-a thing that I have talked about in this chamber on many occasions- we must provide a better product. When we provide a better product-and that is being done today; the product today is much better than it was two years ago or five years ago-a great many of our worries in connection with the fishing industry will be solved, in my opinion.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to detract at all from the assistance that is being given to the fishermen. I see that the next item is a bounty of $160,000. On looking into the bounty I find that it is paid not for catching predatory fish or something of that kind-
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Is the hon. gentleman speaking on item 133 or on the next item?
On item 133.
All right.
I am not sure. I am speaking on this item of $1 million.
That is right.
The bounty which I find in the public accounts was paid not for the destruction of predatory fish or the catching of big fish but for the-
I am afraid the hon. member will find that the bounty has nothing to do with the item that is now under discussion.

I appreciate that fact. It is just a preliminary expression of good will towards the fishermen. I have no objection to it. I appreciate it is paid to the fishermen and boat owners directly. The item under discussion for $1 million is described as providing for technical services to fishermen

and fishing industries. In this chamber I dare say members have become accustomed to very scanty descriptions being given, but when public funds to the amount of $1 million are to be voted on a resolution which is in such indefinite terms as that, particularly after the explanation which has been made by the minister, it seems to me that it is time for the committee to intervene. I would suggest that this item should not be passed in its present form.
Perhaps my nature is unduly suspicious but my suspicions have not been allayed by the statement of the acting minister, or by the fact that the acting minister is here to deal with this item, or by his statement that his electioneering goes on after the campaign. I would be disposed to question this item as being something in the nature of a blank cheque for the acting minister, and it is a fairly substantial one. It seems to me that if the committee is to be asked to provide funds for technical assistance to the fishing industry, for some specific project, it is all very well; let us pass it. But if it is to be described in general terms and put into effect, it leaves the matter open really for the department to spend this money in any way it sees fit. Particularly as this item appears to be intended largely for the province represented by the acting minister, I suggest that it should not carry without more detail being given.

I should like for a moment to speak on this item because I realize what has happened since Newfoundland entered into confederation and became a part of this great Canadian nation. At the time the discussion was going on as to whether or not Newfoundland would become part of Canada one of the arguments used was that in becoming part and parcel of this great nation we could look for greater expansion and also for greater aid and help in industrial matters such as the fisheries. I do not want to repeat what I said the other night when the Minister of Fisheries was here. I realize that tonight he is in Newfoundland, and while he cannot answer questions of hon. members of the house he is answering the questions that are no doubt being put to him by various fishermen there who are greatly interested at this time of the year. Only this morning I received a telegram from Newfoundland saying that the fish had struck in there. Although there has been plenty of ice on the northeast coast from Labrador down to cape Bonavista for several weeks, it seems that the ice has moved off now and we are glad to hear that the fish have moved in. In fact one trap set and hauled yesterday morning produced 25 barrels of fish which was good
Supply-Fisheries
news to the fishermen and good news to me because the season is rather advanced.
The point I should like to make is that we were hoping that by becoming a part of this great nation we would receive every assistance possible in order to utilize to the fullest these great reservoirs of food off the east coast in the Atlantic. I realize what an important item of food fish is and how necessary it is for the body to have a certain amount of protein. We realize that the eating of fish is an admirable way of providing the necessary protein for the body.
But in order to do this thing scientifically, in order to get the very best advantage and the greatest amount of money out of our food resources, naturally some experimentation must take place. I think the Acting Minister of Fisheries has already explained the situation very well. This vote is provided in order to carry on experimentation. Our traditional markets were in the Mediterranean; for centuries past they were provided with fish by the fishermen of Newfoundland in order to supply their needs. That was also true of the West Indies, and there was a time when Newfoundland shipped something over 400,000 quintals of fish to Brazil in one year.
We know that a lot of that has changed with the changing times. Today we have refrigeration and we know that the food value of fish is much better in the fresh form than when it is salted, put out to dry and cure and has to withstand the various vagaries of the weather. The salted fish had to be transported for thousands of miles, then at times taken into the hills and delivered to the people who had to eat the fish perhaps months after it had been caught.
In order to change this situation and bring about a new era through a revolution, so to speak, in fishery development, naturally some money had to be spent. I believe that the committee will agree that this is a move in the right direction. By having mechanical dryers, which have been explained by the hon. member for Charlotte, they will be able to do away with the old method of the fishermen and their wives spreading fish by hand. Now the process will be mechanized, and it is hoped that a larger volume of fish will be caught and processed and a greater number of dollars brought into the Canadian economy than was the case with flake dried salted fish. The end result before was a rather indifferent quality of fish, and we are hoping now that there will be a greater standardization of quality and thus a better article of food.
Of course this can only be done on a large scale by having such things as mechanical

Supply-Fisheries
dryers. We have been delighted to hear the results of the efforts of the Minister of Public Works and the deputy minister of fisheries in concluding trade agreements in Europe. We are delighted that they have made agreements to sell fish from Newfoundland to Portugal, Italy and Spain. We realize that we are dependent upon these foreign markets, but we find that today the situation is different from what it was before we entered confederation because we now have to sell for dollars where before we could sell for sterling. We could arrange sales in sterling in the soft currency markets. The result has been that we have found that there has been a certain lessening of the exports of fish because of the inability of these countries to provide dollars to buy our codfish. Therefore we have to change from salt fish to a certain degree and move in the direction of fresh fish.
There are physical handicaps which will prevent the full utilization of fresh fish plants on the whole of the Newfoundland coast. There are areas where it will still be necessary to salt the cod as it is caught. As I said before, the purpose of the experimentation is to perfect mechanical dryers operated through power. The exposing of Newfoundland fish to the beneficent rays of the sun makes it a very good article of diet. It may be possible through experimentation to develop a method of treating the fish with ultra violet or other rays if the necessary electrical power is available, but these things are matters for research and experimentation.
Personally I am very glad to see this vote. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West, the full amount of the vote was not expended last year. I think we can take it for granted that all expenditures under this vote will be carefully scrutinized and that it will react to the benefit of Newfoundland and other fishermen.

I think I should perhaps say a word in reply to the hon. member for St. Paul's. I think the best way I can do it is by reading two or three extracts from a statement made on October 1, 1953 after a joint discussion between representatives of the government of Newfoundland and the federal government. It reads in part as follows:
The policy of the federal government was outlined as one of undertaking experimental and exploratory work in determining location of fish populations; of experimenting in mechanized handling and processing of light salted fish on which so many shore fishermen depend; of providing normal federal programs such as the construction and maintenance of harbour works and aids to navigation. The federal government will not finance the construction of commercial plants; the facilities of the industrial development bank and other national legislation like the Cold Storage Act are of course available in Newfoundland as elsewhere.

That is a general statement of policy. The actual operation of the program in Newfoundland for this current year was indicated to be as follows:
1.	The construction of a breakwater, necessary dredging, wharves and breastworks-
Some of these things of course are not in this vote but are in public works.
-as the federal part of a plan for all-round community development at La Scie that will cover salt and frozen fish and fish meal operations.
It is not expected to do that in one year. It is going to be installed over several years.
2.	Construction and operation of a federal experimental salt fish plant in the Valleyfield-Badger's Quay area to handle northeast coast light salted fish.
3.	Small-scale centralization and partial mechanization of individual fishermen's curing operations at Quirpon, to serve the fishermen of that area; a similar small-scale development is being planned for Seldom-Come-By.
That place is in my constituency, but is not my motto.
You might consider it.

I continue:
The extension of small community development to other places will depend upon the success of these experiments.
4.	Construction of a fishermen's wharf in St. John's to serve a fresh fish market, which will be provided by provincial or local authorities.
The market itself will be provided locally. Certain indications were given of the normal federal services which would be provided to speed up development.
In order to make this not seem as though it were entirely Newfoundland, perhaps I should complete my answer by giving a break-down of the other allotments. They are as follows: Technical services to fishermen and the fishing industry, $196,000; demonstration and exploration in Newfoundland-that is in connection with long-lining, a certain type of fishing that is still in the experimental stage-$130,000; fish drying experiments, Bonavista, Newfoundland, $200,000; economic survey, Newfoundland- that has been going on for a number of years and this is just this year's commitment- $12,000; herring exploration, maritimes, $40,000; scallop exploration, maritimes, $50,000-1 might note there that a new bed was found in the St. Pierre bank last year; shrimp exploration, British Columbia, $12,000; the Valleyfield fish drying experiment I have already mentioned, $300,000; savings gear experiment, Newfoundland, $10,000; midwater trawl development, British Columbia, $10,000; fish liver hydrolysate (maritimes), $20,000; motorized boats for schooners, maritimes, $20,000; tunnel-stern boats, maritimes,


$5,000. In Newfoundland, I may say, the term "maritimes" is used to mean the other three Atlantic provinces.

I should like to say that my objection was not to the program which the acting minister has now outlined and which I am very glad to have on Hansard. It does give some reasonable explanation for the very large sum. My objection was the blank cheque. The acting minister will agree with me that it is the duty of the opposition not to assume this blank cheque is going to be filled in with the appropriate items.
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman.

I am interested in this Valleyfield project. I understand that the minister has inferred it is going to cost considerably more than the money provided this year, which is $200,000, if my memory serves me well. What does the minister expect the total cost of this project will be when it is completed?
It is expected to complete the plant within this fiscal year, and $300,000 is the estimated cost of the complete plant.
Has part of it already been built?

No, none of it has been built. The site has been chosen and some of the marine works have been surveyed. The last report I had on it was that it was hoped construction could start probably in October. It is not desirable to start construction except for the outside shell until the end of the fishing season because one of the incidental advantages of this kind of program is to do the work, so far as possible, during the winter season when the fishermen cannot fish. I am sure all hon. members will approve of that.
There is still an item in public works estimates referring to this project.
There are some marine works required.
Does the minister know how much the over-all project will cost?
I have not got it at my fingertips, although I should have because it is in my riding.

Item agreed to.

134. Field services administration, $701,900.

On this item of field services administration, protection branch, I should
Supply-Fisheries
like to say a word about a matter which was raised on the first item and discussed at some length. Hon. members may recall that the matter of the operation of trawlers and draggers off our coastline waters was raised at that time, and without repeating what was set forth in Hansard then I may say that we know there were two different conditions under which our trawlers operate. The small ones operated within three miles of our coastline or up to three miles from our coastline, and United States vessels can operate within three miles of our coastline. Canadian-built draggers and trawlers over 65 feet are compelled to remain out over twelve miles from our coastline. This matter was discussed at some length in the house and naturally different views were expressed with respect to it. Some hon. members took the position that this was an injustice to Canadian trawlers in the sense that United States vessels were allowed to operate within three miles of our coastline.
The suggestion was made, therefore, that our department should abrogate this decision and allow Canadian trawlers also to operate within three miles of our coastline. As you are aware, those trawlers which are built with Canadian funds have a condition endorsed on their certificate saying that they must operate outside the twelve-mile limit. I would say, superficially, that that appears to be a proper condition and should continue, whereas some others say that since United States vessels operate within the three-mile limit these Canadian trawlers should also be permitted to operate within the three-mile limit. My answer to that is this. This regulation was not promulgated for the benefit of the trawler operators. It was done to protect the inshore fishermen. Although we could not control the United States trawlers under international law, we could control our own. Our government said, and I say quite properly, that these trawlers should be kept beyond the twelve-mile limit.
I want to express my own protest against any suggestion of abrogating our decision. At the moment the situation for the inshore fishermen is not happy. These United States trawlers are operating within the three-mile limit of our coastline. Sometimes on a foggy night or perhaps if it is not so foggy but the patrol boats are not very near, these United States trawlers quite often can be seen within three hundred yards of our coastline. Our lobster fishermen lose their traps and our inshore fishermen lose their gear because of the operation of these boats. My suggestion is that instead of abrogating this decision so the Canadian trawler can operate within the

Supply-Fisheries
three-mile limit, we should through negotiations through the Department of External Affairs enter into some arrangement whereby the United States trawlers can be kept farther out instead of permitting the Canadian trawler to come closer to shore.
I realize that that is not something that can be accomplished overnight. I am sure the acting minister knows of operations that have taken place in certain countries under which new principles have been laid down for the establishment of inland waters. I believe these new principles are now before the international courts or they have been referred there for settlement. It is quite possible that in the relatively near future we may find international law will permit us to extend our inland waters farther out than the three-mile limit, possibly by adopting the headlands method or the cape to cape method as one country has done. Various expedients have been adopted. If we could establish a different basis for outlining our inland waters than is presently the case, then I believe we would be able to protect our fisheries. I am sure the hon. member for Charlotte would agree with me in that.
I would point out to the Secretary of State, who has more than an academic interest in this because he knows the political history and background of this country, that the particular waters in which he is interested are around Newfoundland, but the ones in which I am interested are in the bay of Fundy.
The situation with respect to that particular water is different from that of any other water on our coastline. Years ago when the British government was in charge of our external relations it took the position that the bay of Fundy formed part of the inland waters of Canada. They maintained that position. And one can go back to the records of the old discussions and the exchange of correspondence between London and Washington and find that position reiterated time and again. The Americans, on the other hand, said it was part of the high seas, and refused to accept that policy.
In the end it was agreed to disagree. Great Britain refused to concede that it was part of the high seas, and the Americans refused to concede that it was part of the inland waterways of Canada. And there the matter stood for many years. One might suggest that there is a proscriptive right; at least the Americans have been allowed to come into those waters. And I am not suggesting for a moment that they should be excluded.
But I do say that our Department of Fisheries should take a very dim view of any suggestion to allow American trawlers to

operate within three miles of our coastline. This matter should be kept in abeyance for a few more years until the international situation is cleared up. Because the plight of our inland fishermen today is serious indeed. They cannot operate against the operations of these trawlers coming along the coastline. I know one must not stand in the way of progress. I am not suggesting that in the matter of our high seas fisheries, or deep water fisheries, we should go back to the schooner days, or any of the methods which were used 20 or 25 years ago. But there are along our shoreline little villages and large villages in which there are thousands upon thousands of people who have lived there for generations, and who are living there today, and whose sole existence is being threatened by the operations of these trawlers.
This is not only true in the bay of Fundy. I see the hon. member from Halifax in his seat. I am sure he will agree with me that, for instance, in the waters of St. Margaret's bay, the same situation exists. Last year I was approached by many fishermen in that district who wanted protests raised with respect to this. They said they were sitting on the shore with rifles in their hands taking pot shots at American trawlers coming within the waters of St. Margaret's bay.
I am sorry to have spent as much time as this at this late hour, but I was rather intrigued by the suggestions which were made. I say it is a matter of absolute injustice to thousands of people along that coast line, and I wish to express my protest again with respect to a suggestion which was made in my absence.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions to ask on the subject of conservation. I shall not speak about the general subject of conservation, because we all realize the importance of it. However we are worried about two or three of our fish products in the bay of Fundy.
First of all, I should like to refer to the clam industry. I am referring particularly to the soft-shelled little neck clams. In Charlotte, and to a lesser degree in Saint John county, there has been a serious depletion in clams. I understand various meetings were held last year asking for a closed season in this clam industry to which I have referred. It was the unanimous opinion of a meeting held in August of 1953 that a closed season should be demanded. I say that we are worried about the serious depletion of clams, and I am wondering what new action has been taken or what inquiries have been made.

I realize that these regulations changes are controversial. Can the minister tell me the position as to the possibility of closing the season for clams?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: This question is now under study by the research board, and officials of our department. No firm decision has been made in the matter, but it is receiving very intensive consideration at the present time.

I should like also to refer to the lobster industry, with which the hon. member for Charlotte dealt earlier. In this connection the worry is the same, and concerns undersized lobsters. Perhaps I might read a headline which would explain the situation. This is a headline appearing in the Telegraph-Journal of Saint John, stating "Maritime Lobster Fishermen Want 'Get-Tough' Policy Used Against Poaching, Taking Undersized Fish". Then the article goes on to explain what happened at the meeting. It says that representatives from the three maritime provinces asked federal authorities for stricter enforcement measures that would deter an increasing black-market operation, which has created a dual price structure on lobsters.
Again I would ask what new action is being taken in connection with the lobster industry. I realize these are continuing problems, but unless new action is taken each year the thing goes on and on, and nothing is done-and then we will not have an industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: As the hon. member for Charlotte has said, this is a continuing problem and one that has been bothering the department for many years. This year a greater effort was made to train the protection officers in the better enforcement of their duties. I think, if we may judge from letters we are receiving at the present time in the department, a better job is being done this year than has been done for many years. At least we hope that is so. But, as the hon. member has mentioned, it is a tremendously difficult job. There are so many ways of circumventing the protection officers, and it is such a lucrative business, that the incentive for illegal practices is very great.

Then, I should like also to refer to the small herring industry. I have here a report which indicates that small herring taken in New Brunswick waters, or waters of the bay of Fundy, are used in the United States for fertilizer and oil. This may be surplus; it may be a wasted part of the industry that would not be sold. But it seems
Supply-Fisheries
outrageous to me that our good fish, particularly the small ones, are being commercialized in this way in the state of Maine, and indeed throughout the New England states .
I should like to hear whether any investigation has been conducted into the matter, and whether there is any truth in this report. If so, what measures are being taken to correct this serious outrage?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I should suggest that it would be difficult to prevent fishermen from selling where they can get the best price. I think the problem is one of economics. If the fishermen find it more profitable to dispose of their fish to American processors, then I do not think we would be justified in interfering.

That was not my point. It is not so much a matter of economics. I am simply saying that this procedure does not seem right. Perhaps if better marketing prices could be obtained for these fish they would not have to sell them as surplus in that way. I take it that the price offered for the herring is not a competitive price under present market conditions. It is simply a left-over price that is given.
In other words, when they see that the herring catch cannot be sold, they dump it on the market in the United States. I am simply suggesting that the whole problem should be investigated, and then it would not be necessary to waste the catch in this way.

I should like to say a word on that point. There is no doubt that last year thousands of tons of small sardines were sold for fertilizer. They were sold in that way because they were too small for canning purposes. When the fish struck on the coastline they were mixed with silver hake, squid and other fish of no value at all. Our fishermen who had waited four or five months to make a few dollars could see a chance to make a few dollars by the sale of fertilizer. There are two sides of the question. Some will argue that small fish should not be taken out of the water. The man who needs a dollar argues, they are mine; I have caught them and I feel I should be given the opportunity of disposing of them if I can get something for them. Thousands of tons of what we would call brit, small herrings, went through as fertilizer. If the department should come out and say to the fishermen, you have got the fish but you cannot sell them, it would be a tough one to put over with them.

Supply-Fisheries
Again, these small fish would have been big fish some day and would be worth a lot more money so that the value would have been very much greater. These are the two sides to the question. It is one that would be most delicate for the Department of Fisheries to deal with, I would say.

Mr. Chairman, I feel in somewhat the same situation as the hon. member for St. Paul's in that it is perhaps unusual for a dry bob-I think that is the word one might use-to get mixed up with the fisheries estimates. But I want to transfer the discussion to the Pacific coast for a moment, but not quite to the coast. Any complaint I have relates to the protective regulations which at present prevent sport fishing for certain types of salmon in our inland waters. It has been a sport for many years in certain reaches of the Fraser river, as well as the Thompson river, to fish for the salmon as they come up the river and while they are still in good condition. That is some considerable time before they reach the spawning beds, at which time they would not of course be fit for consumption; indeed, they would not be any sport to catch.
I might say that I have taken this matter up with the department but regret to have to report that no conclusion has been arrived at. Last year a notice was posted at Lillooet, British Columbia, which is in my riding and where there is quite a favourable stretch of water for fishermen. This was over the printed signature of the deputy minister. The regulation is dated March 2, 1953 and prohibited everyone except an Indian from fishing for, catching or killing a sockeye, pink or chum salmon by any means in the non-tidal waters of the province. In my correspondence with the department I pointed out that in the first place when you are fishing for these types of fish which are legitimate to catch you are fishing with a lure, and unfortunately the sockeye, chum and pink salmon are apparently unable to read the deputy minister's notice, and therefore some of them are ill-advised enough to take those hooks. The notice goes on to say that anyone taking such fish shall return them to the water immediately and if possible uninjured. When you tag a twelve-pound or a fifteen-pound salmon and get him in your boat where you can unhook him and possibly have to gaff him in the process, it is rather difficult to return him to the water uninjured.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You are not even uninjured yourself.

As I pointed out in the correspondence, firstly it is impossible to avoid

hooking these fish if you are fishing for this species which you are allowed to fish.
Secondly, the result of such regulations, if enforced, would be to deprive anglers in the interior of a perfectly legitimate sport. They are fishing for fish in good condition. Thirdly, the type of fishing which was described was fishing with lures, and not jigging or gaffing. It was genuine sport fishing which was the only type sought to be exempted from this regulation.
Fourthly, the enforcement of the regulation could only have the effect of ensuring that there would be returned to the water a number of fish which were bound to die.
In their reply the department made the point that the fish were on their way up to the spawning grounds and that owing to the increase in population and the opening up of certain areas of the province it was found that increasing numbers of those fish were being caught. They go on to say:
Reports of increasing evidence of mutilation and destruction of salmon on or approaching the spawning grounds made clear the need for additional special protection for these spawning stocks.
They also said that in their opinion these particular types of fish, that is, sockeye, pink and chum salmon, are not sport fish. I referred the matter back to the angling association which had taken it up with me and asked them for their opinion, and they report as follows:
In our opinion here, the sockeye is a sport fish. It takes a lure. It treats the fisherman the same as other fish do in that if he has not got the proper lure on his line, then no fish. It is quite true that some are snagged. This of course can and has happened when fishing in lakes and in the salt water. We can produce concrete evidence that at least 60 per cent of the fish are caught by the mouth.
This indicates of course that it is genuine sport fishing. The letter goes on:
You can rest assured that at least 99 per cent of all the fish we have caught by angling are in a prime condition. It has been found that those that are not in a prime condition will not take the lure.
I personally have had present persons who are in the fish canning business when a fish has been landed. The expression used by them was: "These fish are in prime condition, as good as we get on the coast.	,
The department promised to look into it and bring it to the attention of the minister on his return to Ottawa. I regret that I have not had any further answer. I hope that they still have the matter under consideration, but I would add in conclusion that it seems to me to be a matter that justifies review because I hardly think that the number of fish taken by genuine anglers could do conservation any harm. I am not talking about netting or those who may be prepared to

indulge in improper forms of fishing and try to sell them commercially. That can easily be done. It does seem to me unfair that a perfectly legitimate and well-recognized form of sport fishing should be denied to those who live in the interior of our province and who, if this is denied to them, are going to be condemned to eat canned salmon for the rest of their lives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: This is purely a problem of conservation. I can assure the hon. member for Kamloops that it is under consideration at the present time.

I say this with due respect; the simple fact is that I took this up first last August, and I would venture to suggest that the consideration must be approaching some finality at the moment. I hope the parliamentary assistant will assure me that we can expect a decision shortly.

136. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $490,000.

This item deals with the construction of works in connection with the protective services. I should like to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to a matter which has achieved considerable prominence in the press in the maritimes within the last few weeks. I am very sorry indeed that the minister himself is not here, because when he was here and replied to the various speeches which had been made, as I recall it, he gave a lecture on what he termed the birds and the bees, and he directed it primarily to the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. If the minister were here tonight, and if he had read the press on what has happened in Nova Scotia, it might be advisable for him to write a second volume on the birds and the bees and advise us more explicitly than he did that night.
At any rate the department has supervised the construction of a fish ladder at a hydro dam on the Gaspereau river. For some strange reason, after the fish ladder was put up it was found that there was not enough water going down the ladder to enable the fish to go up. I do not have to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that a fish trying to go up a dry fish ladder is busier than a one-armed paper hanger with the itch. He does not accomplish much more. The result was that there were thousands and tens of thousands of papa fish and mama fish swimming around at the mouth of the ladder.
There was a long line waiting to go up the ladder. The mama fish, being in that condition euphemistically known as a delicate state of health, were rather large and slow and they
Supply-Fisheries
stayed relatively still. The papa fish being more slim and active managed to swim away. In the end departmental officials got worried about it and tried to encourage the mama fish to go up the ladder. But they would not go because in fact there was not enough water. So they obtained trucks and tin cans and nets and tried to scoop up the fish. As I said, the mama fish being rather slow did not get away and they dumped them into the tin cans, put them in trucks and drove them up around the ladder and put them back in the water again. Many of the papa fish, being pretty active, got clear. The very interesting question being raised now down in Nova Scotia is what sort of volume the minister would write now on the affairs of the birds and the bees, and they are wondering whether he got enough papa fish in the tin cans and whether the mama fish in the tin cans were very much use after being put in the tin cans. It is questioned whether the mama fish were very useful after being put in the cans.
This raises a very interesting problem. I wonder how many hon. members saw the last issue of Weekend magazine, which was carried in most newspapers across the country, for it showed some coloured photographs of the Gaspereau fish caught in the Gaspereau river, which happens to be in my constituency. The farmers there with their scoop nets actually work for a few weeks in the spring and some years make as high as $10,000 in catching the Gaspereau fish going up the river. If two years from now there are not going to be any fish coming up the river, the farmers who have hitherto earned a fair competence from the fish in that river are going to take a very jaundiced view of the situation.
You can speak about it in a humorous way, Mr. Chairman, but after all this is a serious matter. I think quite frankly it reflects on the service in some way. The fish ladders should certainly be constructed in such a manner that water would be flowing down at all times. The fisheries officials should have seen to it that some remedial steps were taken because there might be almost irretrievable damage done to this most valuable industry which means tens of thousands of dollars to the people in my own constituency. I do hope the minister will see that something is done about this. I know this must have been brought to his attention because it got headlines in the press for some days and the news item was spread all over the country. Farmers came from other parts of the country hoping to scoop up the fish. This is a serious situation and I hope it will be rectified before another year has passed.
Item agreed to.
